kpis.heading: How to read these figures
kpis.intro: The tiles sum up your whole strategy in a few numbers. Most of them show the position at the end of the period, that is at the end of {{lastYear}}. The exceptions: “Capital invested” is your starting capital at the beginning, and “Return per year” sums up the whole period. The first tile with the coloured number is the main result. The text below the tiles repeats the key points in full sentences. Everything here is a model calculation based on the assumptions at the bottom of the page, not a promise.
kpis.introReinvest: The tiles sum up your whole strategy in a few numbers. Most of them show the position at the end of the period, that is at the end of {{lastYear}}. The exceptions: “Capital invested” is your starting capital at the beginning, while “Return per year” and “Capital recycling” sum up the whole period. The first tile with the coloured number is the main result. The text below the tiles repeats the key points in full sentences. Everything here is a model calculation based on the assumptions at the bottom of the page, not a promise.

kNet.label: Net worth at the end
kNet.text: What belongs to you on paper at the end: the value of your apartments minus all outstanding loans, plus money already paid into apartments that are still being built, plus money in the account (liquidity). The table “What your wealth consists of” right below shows how this number is made up. It is not an account balance. Ongoing surpluses only count as far as they are still in the account as liquidity at the end. Without reinvestment that is usually not the case, because the model treats them as if they were paid out to you every year. Costs and taxes of selling the apartments at the end have not been deducted here.

kValue.label: Value of the properties
kValue.text: What all handed-over apartments are worth at the end under the model's assumption. The starting point is each purchase price including VAT, without furniture. From handover onwards this value rises every year by the assumed appreciation of {{g}} % (listed under “Assumptions and notes”). Apartments still under construction at the end are not included. The value is an assumption, not a valuation report and not a guaranteed sale price.

kValueZero.label: Value of the properties
kValueZero.text: What all handed-over apartments are worth at the end under the model's assumption. The starting point is each purchase price including VAT, without furniture. Your plan assumes no appreciation (0 % per year), so the value stays at the purchase price. Apartments still under construction at the end are not included. The value is an assumption, not a valuation report and not a guaranteed sale price.

kUnits.label: Apartments
kUnits.text: How many apartments have been handed over to you and belong to you at the end. An apartment you have bought that is still under construction at the end is not counted yet.

kIrrSale.label: Return per year
kIrrSale.text: Sums up all money flowing between you and the strategy in one number, including compound interest. On one side is what you pay in and when: deposits and instalments from your own capital, the purchase costs and top-ups in years with a minus. On the other side is what you get back and when: the yearly surpluses and, at the end, the proceeds after sale. Imagine a savings account into which you pay exactly these amounts at exactly these times and from which you withdraw them. The return per year is the interest rate this account would have to pay so that it is at exactly zero after the last withdrawal. Experts call this the internal rate of return. It is not the rental yield of a single apartment.

kIrrHold.label: Return per year
kIrrHold.text: Sums up all money flowing between you and the strategy in one number, including compound interest. On one side is what you pay in and when: deposits and instalments from your own capital, the purchase costs and top-ups in years with a minus. On the other side is what you get back and when: the yearly surpluses and, at the end, because nothing is sold, the value of your apartments minus loans (plus money still tied up in apartments under construction), as if you could take it with you at no cost. Imagine a savings account into which you pay exactly these amounts at exactly these times and from which you withdraw them. The return per year is the interest rate this account would have to pay so that it is at exactly zero after the last withdrawal. Experts call this the internal rate of return. It is not the rental yield of a single apartment.

kIrrReinvest.label: Return per year
kIrrReinvest.text: Sums up what you pay in and what it turns into by the end, including compound interest. With reinvestment nothing is paid out along the way, all surpluses stay in the strategy. So the calculation works like this: your starting capital at the beginning and, if agreed, monthly top-ups are set against your net worth at the end. The return per year is the interest rate a savings account would have to pay to turn the same payments into the same end result. Experts call this the internal rate of return. Costs and taxes of a sale at the end have not been deducted. It is not the rental yield of a single apartment.

kEquity.label: Capital invested
kEquity.text: Your starting capital for this strategy. It pays for deposits and instalments. The purchase costs come on top: in the model a flat 1 % of the purchase price including VAT, without furniture. Top-ups in years with a minus are not included here either.

kEquityReinvest.label: Capital invested
kEquityReinvest.text: Your starting capital for this strategy. It pays for deposits, instalments and purchase costs of the first apartments. The model sets the purchase costs at a flat 1 % of the purchase price including VAT, without furniture. Whatever is left stays in the account, including the minimum reserve. Monthly top-ups are not included here.

kDebt.label: Loan at the end
kDebt.text: Everything you still owe at the end: the remaining balance of the bank loans and, where they exist, instalments to the developer still open after handover, an open loan for instalments your own capital does not cover (bridge loan), and additional loans from refinancing. Refinancing means a new loan on an apartment that has already been handed over. The same number appears again under “Financing and borrowing”.

kRecycle.label: Capital recycling
kRecycle.text: Only appears for a strategy with reinvestment. Shows how much equity for further apartments came out of your cash pot, relative to your starting capital. The cash pot is filled by rental surpluses, VAT refunds, sale proceeds, monthly top-ups and the part of the starting capital that did not go into the first apartments. What counts is the equity paid in the year of purchase. Money from refinancing does not count, because it is a new loan. 0,5× means: an amount equal to half of your starting capital went into further apartments this way. It is neither a return nor a profit.

kExit.label: Proceeds after sale
kExit.text: Appears because a sale of all apartments at the end of the period is included. This is what you keep from the sale: sale price minus loan, minus the costs for agent and lawyer (each plus 19 % VAT) and for the transfer levy, minus taxes on the sale{{firma}}. The individual items are listed in the section “What is left after the sale”.

kExitVat.label: Proceeds after sale
kExitVat.text: Appears because a sale of all apartments at the end of the period is included. This is what you keep from the sale: sale price minus loan, minus the costs for agent and lawyer (each plus 19 % VAT) and for the transfer levy, minus the pro rata repayment of the VAT refund, minus taxes on the sale{{firma}}. About the VAT: if you get the VAT refunded for short-term letting and sell within ten years of handover, you have to pay part of it back. If the refund has not arrived yet at the time of sale, you still receive the remaining part, and then this item increases the proceeds. The individual items are listed in the section “What is left after the sale”.

kCash.label: Liquidity at the end
kCash.text: Appears because no sale is included: the money in the account at the end of the model. Without reinvestment this is usually 0 €. The model treats the yearly surpluses as if they were paid out to you every year, so they do not pile up here. An amount only appears here if instalments to the developer are still open at the end and money has been set aside for them.

kCashReinvest.label: Liquidity at the end
kCashReinvest.text: The money in the account at the end of the model. With reinvestment this is the strategy's cash pot: surpluses collect here, and equity for further purchases is paid from here. The minimum reserve also sits here.

kText.label: Text below the tiles
kText.text: The text below the tiles is shown in German. It sums up the starting capital you begin with, how many apartments have been handed over at the end and what they are worth by then.

kTextSale.label: Text below the tiles
kTextSale.text: The text below the tiles is shown in German. It sums up the starting capital you begin with, how many apartments have been handed over at the end and what they are worth by then. It also mentions the sale that is included. What the sale brings you is shown under “Proceeds after sale”.

kTextReinvest.label: Text below the tiles
kTextReinvest.text: The text below the tiles is shown in German. It sums up the starting capital you begin with, how many apartments have been handed over at the end and what they are worth by then. If further apartments are added, it also names the refinancings and how much additional loan is taken out through them. That loan is borrowed money, not profit.

kNetReinvest.label: Net worth at the end
kNetReinvest.text: What belongs to you on paper at the end: the value of your apartments minus all outstanding loans, plus money already paid into apartments that are still being built, plus money in the account (liquidity). The table “What your wealth consists of” right below shows how this number is made up. It is not an account balance. With reinvestment the ongoing surpluses stay in the strategy: at the end they are either in the account as liquidity or tied up as equity in further apartments. Costs and taxes of selling the apartments at the end have not been deducted here.

kValueNeg.label: Value of the properties
kValueNeg.text: What all handed-over apartments are worth at the end under the model's assumption. The starting point is each purchase price including VAT, without furniture. Your plan assumes that this value falls by {{g}} % every year from handover onwards (listed under “Assumptions and notes”). Apartments still under construction at the end are not included. The value is an assumption, not a valuation report and not a guaranteed sale price.

kEquityUnused.label: Capital invested
kEquityUnused.text: Your starting capital for this strategy. In your case it covers everything the apartments need from your own money: deposits, instalments and the purchase costs are paid from it. The model sets the purchase costs at a flat 1 % of the purchase price including VAT, without furniture. Top-ups in years with a minus are not included here.

kTextReinvest0.label: Text below the tiles
kTextReinvest0.text: The text below the tiles is shown in German. It sums up the starting capital you begin with, how many apartments have been handed over at the end and what they are worth by then. If further apartments are added, it also names the refinancings. In your case it says “0 Refinanzierungen” (0 refinancings) and 0 €: no additional loan is taken out on apartments already handed over to pay for the further apartments. Their equity comes from the cash pot.

kNetPays.label: Net worth at the end
kNetPays.text: What belongs to you on paper at the end: the value of your apartments minus all outstanding loans, plus money already paid into apartments that are still being built, plus money in the account (liquidity). The table “What your wealth consists of” right below shows how this number is made up. It is not an account balance. Ongoing surpluses only count as far as they pay instalments to the developer or are still in the account as liquidity at the end. The model treats the rest as if it were paid out to you every year. Costs and taxes of selling the apartments at the end have not been deducted here.

pitfalls.notCash: Net worth is not an account balance. Only the liquidity is available right away, the rest is tied up in the apartments.
pitfalls.netVsExit: Net worth at the end and proceeds after sale are two different numbers. The first is the position before the sale, the second is what is left after all deductions of the sale.
pitfalls.irr: Return per year is not the rental yield, nor “profit divided by years”. It takes into account when which money flows.
pitfalls.equityNotAll: Capital invested is not everything you pay. Without reinvestment the purchase costs come on top, and in years with a minus you add some more.
pitfalls.debtMore: Loan at the end is more than the bank loan: open instalments to the developer, a bridge loan and loans from refinancing count too.
pitfalls.recycle: Capital recycling of 1,0× does not mean your money has doubled. It only means an amount equal to your starting capital went into further apartments.
pitfalls.cashZero: Without reinvestment “Liquidity at the end” almost always shows 0 €. That does not mean you have no money at the end: the surpluses of the individual years count as already paid out.
pitfalls.valueAssumption: The value of the properties is an assumption with a fixed appreciation per year, not a valuation report and not a guaranteed sale price.
pitfalls.model: All numbers are a model calculation. Appreciation, rents, interest and taxes may turn out differently.
pitfalls.equityTopUps: Capital invested is not everything you pay: in years with a minus you add some more.

balance.heading: How to read this table
balance.intro: The table shows what your net worth is made of at the end of the period ({{lastYear}}). Its row labels are shown in German; the explanations below give their meaning. It is a calculation from top to bottom: value of the apartments minus outstanding loans gives your equity in the apartments, the first total in bold. Then the money in the account is added. At the very bottom is the result, the net worth. A minus in front of a number means: this amount is deducted.
balance.introCommitted: The table shows what your net worth is made of at the end of the period ({{lastYear}}). Its row labels are shown in German; the explanations below give their meaning. It is a calculation from top to bottom: value of the apartments minus outstanding loans gives your equity in the apartments, the first total in bold. Then the money already paid into apartments under construction and the money in the account are added. At the very bottom is the result, the net worth. A minus in front of a number means: this amount is deducted.

bValue.label: Wert der Immobilien
bValue.text: (Value of the properties) What all handed-over apartments are worth at the end under the model's assumption: the purchase price including VAT, without furniture, changed every year from handover by the assumed appreciation. The same number as in the tile above.

bDebt.label: Offene Kredite
bDebt.text: (Outstanding loans) Everything you still owe at the end: the remaining balance of the bank loans and, where they exist, instalments to the developer still open after handover, a bridge loan for instalments and loans from refinancing. The same number as “Loan at the end” above.

bEquity.label: Eigenkapital in den Immobilien
bEquity.text: (Equity in the properties) Value minus outstanding loans. This is the part of the apartments that economically belongs to you. Equity here does not mean “the money you paid in”, but “what belongs to you at the end”. It is tied up in bricks: you can only get at it by selling or taking out a new loan.

bCommitted.label: In der Bauphase gebundenes Kapital
bCommitted.text: (Capital tied up during construction) Only appears if an apartment is still under construction at the end. These are the instalments due on those apartments up to the end. The model counts them at the amount paid, without appreciation. Only from handover does the apartment count with its value and its loan.

bCash.label: Liquidität
bCash.text: (Liquidity) Money in the account at the end. Only this part is available right away. Without reinvestment it is usually 0 €, because the model treats each year's surpluses as paid out to you. If an amount does appear, it is money that was set aside for later instalments to the developer.

bCashReinvest.label: Liquidität
bCashReinvest.text: (Liquidity) Money in the account at the end. Only this part is available right away. With reinvestment this is the strategy's cash pot, which also holds the minimum reserve.

bNet.label: Netto-Vermögen
bNet.text: (Net worth) The total of the rows above: equity in the properties plus capital tied up during construction (if any) plus liquidity. The same number as in the first tile above. Costs and taxes of a sale at the end have not been deducted here.

wealth.heading: How to read this chart
wealth.intro: For every year from {{first}} to {{last}} the chart shows four lines, each with the position at the end of the year. The years run across, the amounts in euros run up: “k” means thousand (500k is 500.000 €), “Mio” means million. The dots on the right edge show the final position. On a computer, move the mouse over a year to see that year's exact numbers.

wValue.label: Value of the properties
wValue.text: Blue line. What all handed-over apartments are worth in each year under the model's assumption. In the year of a handover it jumps up, because from then on the apartment counts with its value (purchase price including VAT, without furniture). After that it changes every year by the assumed appreciation. During construction the model assumes no change in value.

wValueSale.label: Value of the properties
wValueSale.text: Blue line. What all handed-over apartments are worth in each year under the model's assumption. In the year of a handover it jumps up, because from then on the apartment counts with its value (purchase price including VAT, without furniture). After that it changes every year by the assumed appreciation. During construction the model assumes no change in value. In the year of a sale, value and loan of the apartment sold drop out.

wDebt.label: Loan
wDebt.text: Coral line. What you owe in total in each year: bank loans, instalments to the developer still open after handover, a bridge loan for instalments and loans from refinancing. It rises when a loan is added, usually in the year of a handover: from then on that apartment's loan counts. After that it falls through repayment and through instalments paid to the developer.

wEquity.label: Equity in the properties
wEquity.text: Green line. Value minus loan, that is the gap between the blue and the coral line. This is the part of the handed-over apartments that belongs to you. It grows when the value rises or the loan falls.

wNet.label: Net worth
wNet.text: Grey dashed line. Equity in the properties plus money already paid into apartments under construction, plus liquidity in the account. The gap between the grey and the green line is exactly this money under construction and in the account. If no apartment is under construction and there is no money in the account, the two lines lie on top of each other.

ex.start: {{y0}} is the first year in which none of your apartments is under construction. Your apartments are then worth {{v0}}, the loan stands at {{d0}}. Your equity in the properties: {{v0}} minus {{d0}} equals {{e0}}.
ex.valueUp: By {{yN}} the value rises to {{vN}}, an increase of {{dv}}{{purchaseNote}}.
ex.valueDown: By {{yN}} the value falls to {{vN}}, a decrease of {{dv}}.
ex.debtDown: The loan falls to {{dN}}, a decrease of {{dd}}{{note}}.
ex.debtUp: The loan rises to {{dN}}, an increase of {{dd}}{{note}}.
ex.eqUp: Together your equity in the properties grows by {{de}} to {{eN}} ({{calc}}).
ex.eqDown: Together your equity in the properties falls by {{de}} to {{eN}} ({{calc}}).
ex.debtNoteDown: (on balance, because loans for further purchases are added along the way)
ex.debtNoteUp: , because loans for further purchases are added

m.markers: Vertical dashed lines marked “Purchase” or “Sale” show the years in which the model buys a further apartment or sells one.
m.firstBelow: In the first year ({{y0}}) your net worth is {{nw0}}, which is below your starting capital of {{ek}}. This is not a loss. In this year the model only counts what has already gone into the apartments{{cashPart}}. Equity that is only meant for later instalments does not show up in any line in this year. Purchase costs are not an asset and are not in any line.
m.firstBelowCash: , plus the money in the account
m.negEquity: {{when}} the green line is below zero: the loan is then already higher than the value of the handed-over apartments, because it also pays instalments for apartments under construction. Those apartments only count with their value from handover. The instalments paid are part of the grey line, which is why the net worth is still above zero.
m.dropHandover: In {{y}} the net worth falls by {{drop}}. An apartment is handed over in this year. From then on its value minus its loan counts instead of the instalments paid. A furniture package bought with it is not part of the value, and appreciation only starts at handover. That is why the number can dip slightly in the year of handover.
m.dropModel: In {{y}} the net worth falls by {{drop}}. A further apartment bought in the model is handed over in this year. During its construction the model counts the instalments due in full as tied-up capital, including the part the bank loan will pay later. No loan for this appears in the coral line during that time. This lifts the grey line during construction. From handover its value minus the bank loan counts, which is why the number drops in this year.
m.heldVat: In {{y}} the grey line is {{cash}} above the green one. This is money from rent and VAT refund that stays in the account for the next instalments to the developer.
m.heldRent: In {{y}} the grey line is {{cash}} above the green one. This is money from rent that stays in the account for the next instalments to the developer.
m.sale: The lines end in {{lastYear}} with the position immediately before the sale. What is left after the sale is shown in the tile “Proceeds after sale” above: {{exitNet}}.
m.purchases1: The dashed line marked “Purchase” is at {{years}}. In this year the model buys a further apartment. The equity for it comes first from the account and, where that is not enough, from an additional loan on an apartment that has already been handed over (refinancing). With the refinancing, and at the latest with the handover of the new apartment, the coral line therefore rises.
m.purchasesN: The dashed lines marked “Purchase” are at {{years}}. In each of these years the model buys a further apartment. The equity for it comes first from the account and, where that is not enough, from an additional loan on an apartment that has already been handed over (refinancing). With the refinancing, and at the latest with the handover of the new apartment, the coral line therefore rises.
m.sales1: The line marked “Sale” is at {{years}}. From this year on, value and loan of the apartment sold are missing from the lines. What is left after the sale sits in the account as liquidity and is therefore part of the grey line.
m.salesN: The lines marked “Sale” are at {{years}}. From these years on, value and loan of the apartments sold are missing from the lines. What is left after a sale sits in the account as liquidity and is therefore part of the grey line.
m.dropOpLoss: In addition, in {{y}} the income does not cover costs, interest and taxes. The shortfall is paid from the account and lowers the net worth further.

pitfalls.gapNotGain: The gap between the blue and the coral line is your equity, not your profit. What you paid in for it is included.
pitfalls.greyNotCash: The grey line is not an account balance.
pitfalls.blueAssumption: The blue line is an assumption with a fixed appreciation per year. In reality prices fluctuate, including downwards.
pitfalls.jump: If the blue and the coral line both jump up in the same year, that is usually a handover: from then on the apartment's value and its loan count. Neither money nor debt has appeared out of nowhere.
pitfalls.startBelow: If the grey line starts below your starting capital, no money has been lost. The model does not yet count equity that is only meant for later instalments in those years.
pitfalls.yearEnd: Each point is the position at the end of the year. The chart does not show what happens during a year.
pitfalls.surplusMissing: Without reinvestment the freely available surpluses of the individual years are missing from the grey line. They count as paid out and are shown in the “Cash flow” column in the section “What the portfolio produces year by year”.

financing.heading: How to read the figures and the chart
financing.intro: The four tiles describe your financing. “Loan at the end” and “Loan to value (LTV)” show the position at the end of the period, “Total interest” and “Total repayment” are totals in euros over all years. If you move the mouse over “Loan to value (LTV)”, a short explanation appears. The chart “Loan and borrowing room” uses the coral line to show for every year how much you owe in total at the end of the year. The years run across, the amounts in euros run up (“k” means thousand, “Mio” means million). On a computer, move the mouse over a year to see the exact numbers.
financing.introReinvest: The four tiles describe your financing. “Loan at the end” and “Loan to value (LTV)” show the position at the end of the period, “Total interest” and “Total repayment” are totals in euros over all years. If you move the mouse over “Loan to value (LTV)”, a short explanation appears. The chart “Loan and borrowing room” uses the coral line to show for every year how much you owe in total at the end of the year. The green line also shows how much further loan would be possible on your apartments under the model's assumptions. The years run across, the amounts in euros run up (“k” means thousand, “Mio” means million). On a computer, move the mouse over a year to see the exact numbers.
financing.introNoChart: The four tiles describe your financing. “Loan at the end” and “Loan to value (LTV)” show the position at the end of the period, “Total interest” and “Total repayment” are totals in euros over all years. If you move the mouse over “Loan to value (LTV)”, a short explanation appears. The chart “Loan and borrowing room” stays empty because the period covers only one year.

fDebt.label: Loan at the end
fDebt.text: Everything you still owe at the end of the period: the remaining balance of the bank loans and, where they exist, instalments to the developer still open after handover, an open bridge loan for instalments and loans from refinancing. The same number as above under “Your result at a glance”.

fLtv.label: Loan to value (LTV)
fLtv.text: LTV stands for “loan to value”, the loan relative to the value. The calculation is: loan at the end divided by the value of the properties at the end, in percent. Example: a loan of 600.000 € on a value of 1.000.000 € is 60 %. The smaller the number, the bigger the part that belongs to you. The number applies to all apartments together.

fInterest.label: Total interest
fInterest.text: All interest over the whole period, in euros: for the bank loans, for the instalments to the developer after handover (if the payment plan charges interest on them), for a bridge loan during construction and for loans from refinancing. Interest is a real cost: this money is gone. It is the total of the “Interest” column over all years in the table “What the portfolio produces year by year”. The same number appears under “What the strategy costs you” as “Interest over the period”.

fAmort.label: Total repayment
fAmort.text: How much you pay back on the bank loans and on loans from refinancing over the whole period. Repayment is not an expense like interest: the money leaves your account, but your debt falls by exactly this amount and your equity rises accordingly. Not included are instalments to the developer, the replacement of a bridge loan by the bank loan and the repayment on a sale. It is the total of the “Repayment” column over all years in the table “What the portfolio produces year by year”.

cDebt.label: Loan
cDebt.text: The coral line in the chart: your loan at the end of each year, made up as in “Loan at the end”. It rises when an apartment is handed over or a new loan is added. It falls through repayment and through instalments paid to the developer.

cCap.label: Additional borrowing capacity
cCap.text: The green line, only for a strategy with reinvestment. For each apartment that has been handed over and fully paid to the developer, the model calculates: assumed borrowing limit of {{l}} % times the apartment's value, minus the loans already on it. The results for all apartments are added up. {{adj}} It is measured before any refinancing in the same year. This is a possible additional loan, not a credit balance. Whether and how much a bank actually lends is up to the bank.

ex.loans: For your apartments you take out bank loans of {{loans}} in total (on the cards under “Your apartments” in the “Loan” row).
ex.loansCredit: By the end of {{lastYear}} you have drawn {{loans}} of loan in total for instalments on your apartments (on the cards under “Your apartments” in the “Loan drawn so far” row).
ex.refi: On top of that come {{refi}} from refinancing.
ex.amort: By the end of {{lastYear}} you repay {{amort}} of it. {{loans}} minus {{amort}} equals {{debtEnd}}, exactly your loan at the end.
ex.amortRefi: By the end of {{lastYear}} you repay {{amort}} of it in total. {{loans}} plus {{refi}} minus {{amort}} equals {{debtEnd}}, exactly your loan at the end.
ex.ltv: And the loan to value: {{debtEnd}} divided by {{value}} value of the properties equals {{ltv}}.
ex.year: At the end of {{yPrev}} your loan stands at {{dPrev}}. In {{y}} you repay {{amort}} (“Repayment” column in the table “What the portfolio produces year by year”{{hint}}). {{dPrev}} minus {{amort}} equals {{d}}, exactly the loan at the end of {{y}}. So in this year the loan falls through repayment only.
ex.allYears: , you can see all years via “Show all years” in the section “How your portfolio grows”
ex.ltvOnly: {{debtEnd}} loan at the end divided by {{value}} value of the properties equals a loan to value of {{ltv}}.
ex.loansMixed: For your apartments you take out {{loans}} of loans in total: bank loans and loan drawn for instalments by the end of {{lastYear}} (on the cards under “Your apartments” in the “Loan” and “Loan drawn so far” rows).
ex.amortNone: Nothing is repaid within the period, so this is exactly your loan at the end.
ex.amortNoneRefi: {{loans}} plus {{refi}} equals {{debtEnd}}, exactly your loan at the end. Nothing is repaid within the period.

m.ltv: A loan to value of {{ltv}} means: of every 100 € of property value, about {{ltvR}} € is still financed by loans at the end, and about {{rest}} € belongs to you.
m.ltv0: The loan to value shows 0 % even though there is a loan: no apartment has been handed over yet at the end, and without a property value the model does not calculate a loan to value.
m.interest: Over the period you pay {{interest}} in interest and repay {{amort}}. The interest is a real cost, that money is gone. The repayment builds up your equity.
m.interestNoAmort: Over the period you pay {{interest}} in interest. The interest is a real cost, that money is gone. No repayment falls due within the period.
m.interestHigher: It is normal for interest to be higher than repayment at the start of a financing: with an annuity loan (a constant payment made up of interest and repayment) the interest share is large at first and the repayment share small.
m.interestDev: The interest total also includes interest on the instalments to the developer after handover. Repayment does not reduce this debt, paying the instalments does.
m.saleDebt: Your plan includes a sale at the end of {{lastYear}}. The loan of {{debtEnd}} is then repaid from the sale price and has already been deducted in “Proceeds after sale”. After that no more interest is due on it.
m.holdDebt: Without a sale the loan of {{debtEnd}} continues after {{lastYear}}. Interest and repayment after that are not included in the totals here.
m.gap: Your loan at the end is {{gap}} higher than “all loans minus repayment”. These are amounts still open at the end that are not yet a bank loan: instalments to the developer still open after handover, or a bridge loan for instalments. They are not reduced by repayment, but by paying the instalments, by the bank loan or on a sale.
m.gapNegSale: Your loan at the end is {{gap}} lower than “all loans minus repayment”. The reason: the loans of apartments sold are repaid on the sale, and that does not count as repayment.
m.gapNegUnpaid: Your loan at the end is {{gap}} lower than “all loans minus repayment”. The reason: part of the bank loans on the apartment cards has not been paid out yet at the end of the period.
m.refi: {{refi}} of your loans comes from refinancing. These are additional loans on apartments already handed over, used to pay for further purchases. They increase your debt and cost interest, which is included in “Total interest”.
m.debtStart: Already at the end of {{y}} there is a loan of {{d}}.
m.whyHandover1: {{when}} an apartment is handed over. From then on its bank loan counts towards the loan, plus, if agreed, the instalments to the developer still open and a loan for instalments your own capital does not cover.
m.whyHandoverEach: {{when}} one apartment is handed over each year. From then on its bank loan counts towards the loan, plus, if agreed, the instalments to the developer still open and a loan for instalments your own capital does not cover.
m.whyHandoverN: {{when}} apartments are handed over. From then on their bank loans count towards the loan, plus, if agreed, instalments to the developer still open and a loan for instalments your own capital does not cover.
m.whyRefi: {{when}} the model takes out additional loans on apartments already handed over (refinancing) to buy further apartments.
m.whyModel1: {{when}} a further apartment bought in the model is handed over. From then on its bank loan counts towards the loan.
m.whyModelEach: {{when}} one further apartment bought in the model is handed over each year. From then on its bank loan counts towards the loan.
m.whyModelN: {{when}} further apartments bought in the model are handed over. From then on their bank loans count towards the loan.
m.whyOther: {{when}} your own capital and surpluses are not enough for all instalments due. A loan finances the rest.
m.devPaid1: {{when}} the loan falls by {{extra}} more than repayment alone explains. In this year instalments to the developer after handover are paid, and every instalment paid reduces the debt.
m.devPaidN: {{when}} the loan falls by {{extra}} in total more than repayment alone explains. In these years instalments to the developer after handover are paid, and every instalment paid reduces the debt.
m.peak: Your loan is highest in {{yMax}} at {{dMax}}.
m.noCapLine: Without reinvestment the model does not take out additional loans on apartments already handed over. That is why the chart only has the coral line.
m.capEnd: At the end ({{yN}}) an additional loan of {{cap}} would be possible on paper.{{calc}} This is not a credit balance but a possible new loan, which the bank decides on.
m.capCalc: Calculation: {{l}} % of {{value}} value is {{max}}, minus {{debt}} loan equals {{cap}}.
m.cap0: {{when}} the green line is at 0. At that point no apartment has been handed over and fully paid to the developer yet, or the loans are already at the assumed limit.
m.refiYears: {{when}} there is a refinancing. The green line shows the room before the new financing. The part used appears in the same year as additional loan in the coral line.
m.capAdjNone: In your plan the model assumes no bank valuation discount and counts the full room.
m.capAdjBv: In your plan the bank values the apartments at {{bv}} % of their value (valuation discount).
m.capAdjU: In your plan the model counts {{u}} % of it as usable.
m.capAdjBoth: In your plan the bank values the apartments at {{bv}} % of their value (valuation discount), and the model counts {{u}} % of the result as usable.
m.capCalcAdj: Calculation: {{bv}} % of {{value}} value is {{bankValue}}, {{l}} % of that is {{max}}, minus {{debt}} loan equals {{room}}, and {{u}} % of that equals {{cap}}.
m.ltvPart: A loan to value of {{ltv}} means: for every 100 € of property value there is about {{ltvR}} € of loan at the end.
m.ltvOver: A loan to value of {{ltv}} means: at the end the loan is higher than the value of your handed-over apartments. For every 100 € of property value there is about {{ltvR}} € of loan.
m.ltvCommitted1: Note: the loan also includes money for instalments on an apartment that is still under construction. Its value only counts from handover. That is why the loan to value looks higher than the financing of the handed-over apartments alone.
m.ltvCommittedN: Note: the loan also includes money for instalments on apartments that are still under construction. Their value only counts from handover. That is why the loan to value looks higher than the financing of the handed-over apartments alone.
m.interestBridge: The interest total also includes interest on a bridge loan that pays instalments during construction. The ongoing repayment does not reduce it.
m.interestDevBridge: The interest total also includes interest on the instalments to the developer after handover and on a bridge loan that pays instalments during construction. The ongoing repayment reduces neither of them.
m.whyHandoverNoLoan1: {{when}} an apartment without a bank loan is handed over. From then on, instalments to the developer still open count towards the loan, if there are any, as does a loan for instalments if your own capital does not cover them.
m.whyHandoverNoLoanEach: {{when}} one apartment without a bank loan is handed over each year. From then on, instalments to the developer still open count towards the loan, if there are any, as does a loan for instalments if your own capital does not cover them.
m.whyHandoverNoLoanN: {{when}} apartments without a bank loan are handed over. From then on, instalments to the developer still open count towards the loan, if there are any, as does a loan for instalments if your own capital does not cover them.
m.whyOtherEquity: {{when}} your own capital is not enough for all instalments due. A bridge loan finances the rest.
m.devSurplusVat1: Exactly these {{extra}} come from rent and VAT refund. You can see the same on the card under “Your apartments” in the row “from rent and VAT refund”.
m.devSurplusVatN: Exactly these {{extra}} come from rent and VAT refund. If you add up the rows “from rent and VAT refund” on the cards under “Your apartments”, you get the same amount.
m.devSurplusRent1: Exactly these {{extra}} come from rent. You can see the same on the card under “Your apartments” in the row “from rent”.
m.devSurplusRentN: Exactly these {{extra}} come from rent. If you add up the rows “from rent” on the cards under “Your apartments”, you get the same amount.
m.hiddenBoth: {{hi}} of interest and {{ha}} of repayment in total

pitfalls.amortNotCost: Repayment is not an expense like interest. It reduces your debt by the same amount it costs your account.
pitfalls.interestSum: “Total interest” is a total in euros over all years, not the interest rate. You will find the assumed interest rate under “Assumptions and notes”.
pitfalls.debtNotLoansMinusAmort: Loan at the end is not always “all loans minus total repayment”. Open instalments to the developer and a bridge loan count towards the loan, but they are not reduced by repayment.
pitfalls.ltvAverage: The loan to value is an average across all apartments. A single apartment can carry a higher or lower loan.
pitfalls.ltvModelValue: The loan to value uses the value assumed in the model. A bank uses its own valuation.
pitfalls.rounding: If you add up the “Interest” column yourself, rounding can lead to a difference of a few euros.
pitfalls.handoverJump: If the coral line rises sharply in the year of a handover, that is not new debt out of nowhere: from handover the apartment counts with its loan, and at the same time its value counts in the chart “Value, loan and equity”.
pitfalls.fasterThanAmort: If the loan falls by more than the repayment in a year, there was no sudden extra repayment. Instead, for example, instalments to the developer were paid.
pitfalls.capNotCash: The green line is not a credit balance. It shows how much additional loan would be possible on paper. Using it means more debt and more interest.
pitfalls.capAssumption: The assumed borrowing limit is an assumption for the calculation, not a commitment by any bank.
pitfalls.capOnlyPaid: Only apartments that have been handed over and fully paid to the developer count for the green line. Apartments under construction are no security for a loan.
pitfalls.roundingReinvest: If you add up the “Interest” column yourself, rounding can lead to a difference of a few euros. At first the table does not show every year. To see all years, click “Show all years” in the section “How your portfolio grows”.
pitfalls.roundingHidden: If you add up the “Interest” and “Repayment” columns yourself, rounding can lead to a difference of a few euros. Also, the table does not show every year, only the years with rent and a few key years, at most 12 rows. In your case the hidden years contain {{part}}. They are still included in “Total interest” and “Total repayment”.

cashflow.heading: How to read the cash flow chart and table
cashflow.intro: Cash flow means: money that comes in during a year minus money that goes out. The chart “{{chart}}” shows only the result for each year, the table below shows what it is made of. Each row is one calendar year for all apartments together. From left to right you see what comes in (rent), what goes out (costs, interest, repayment, taxes), what is added once (VAT refund) and, on the far right, the result: the cash flow. A minus in front of a number means this amount goes out. A plus means it comes in. An empty cell means 0 €.

chart.label: Cash flow per year
chart.text: The chart above the table. Each bar is one calendar year and shows exactly the number from the Cash flow column. The chart shows every year, even if the table leaves out some years. The numbers on the left are euros: k means thousand (50k is 50.000 €), Mio means million. The darker horizontal line is zero. With many years, not every bar has a year written below it, but there is a bar for every year. On a computer, move the mouse over a bar to see the year and the exact amount.

pos.label: Surplus
pos.text: Green bar pointing up: money is left over this year. The rent has covered all running payments. If there is a VAT refund or a tax saving that year, it counts too.

neg.label: Top-up
neg.text: Orange-brown bar pointing down: you add this much of your own money this year, because the money from the apartments does not cover all running payments.

cum.label: cumulative
cum.text: Cumulative means added up. The blue line adds up the bars year by year. Its value in a given year is the cash flow of all years up to then. A year with a surplus lifts it, a year with a top-up lowers it. If it is below zero, you have put in more money up to that point than has come out.

year.label: Year
year.text: A calendar year from January to December, not a year counted from the purchase. The table starts with the year of your first purchase contract ({{first}}) and runs to the end of the plan ({{last}}).

rent.label: Rent
rent.text: All rental income of the year for all apartments together. An apartment only earns rent from its handover, that is from the month in which it is finished and handed over to you. In the handover year only the months from the handover count. For holiday letting with a seasonal calculation (occupancy and price per season), the model spreads the annual rent over the months: summer months bring a lot, winter months little. Months in which you use the apartment yourself bring no rent.

costs.label: Costs
costs.text: The running costs of the apartments: management (letting and looking after the apartment, usually a percentage of the rent, otherwise a fixed monthly amount), the building's community fees and the maintenance reserve, money put aside for future repairs. These costs start at the handover, the community fees even while the apartment is empty. Interest and taxes have their own columns. Purchase costs such as lawyer and fees at the time of buying are not in this table.

interest.label: Interest
interest.text: Interest is the price of borrowed money. It does not reduce your loan, this money is gone. The column shows all interest of the year together: for your bank loan, for credit you draw step by step before the monthly loan payment starts in order to pay instalments that are due, and for instalments you still pay to the developer after the handover, if the developer charges interest on them. The developer is the company that builds the apartment and sells it to you.

amort.label: Repayment
amort.text: Repayment is the part of your loan payment that pays back the loan. The money leaves your account, but your debt goes down by the same amount. So it is not lost: the part of the apartment that really belongs to you grows. The monthly payment of your bank loan stays the same; within it the interest share gets smaller every year and the repayment larger. Instalments to the developer are not in this column, and neither is the remaining loan that is paid back in one go when you sell.

tax.label: Taxes
tax.text: All taxes and levies on this year's rental income, calculated for all apartments together, not per apartment.

vat.label: VAT refund
vat.text: VAT means value added tax. When you buy a new apartment in Cyprus, it is included in the purchase price. If you let short-term to holiday guests, you get it back in the model, 18 months after the handover. The table shows it in the year in which these 18 months are reached. It is a one-off amount per apartment, not a running income. If you use the apartment yourself for some months a year, you only get the corresponding part back.

toPay.label: for instalments
toPay.text: This column exists because you still pay instalments to the developer after the handover of a financed apartment. From this handover (for an apartment that is already finished: from the purchase) until the last of these instalments, every surplus goes into a pot. Surplus here means: rent minus costs, interest, repayment and taxes.

net.label: Cash flow
net.text: With a minus in front (orange-brown), you add this much of your own money this year. Not included are: payments towards the purchase price from {{ek}} or from a loan, purchase costs, the increase in value of the apartments and the proceeds from a sale. The bars in the chart show exactly this column.

ex.start: The year {{year}} from your table: your apartments bring in {{rent}} in rent.
ex.pot: {{v}} goes into the pot for instalments.
ex.potBack: {{v}} flows back to you from the pot for instalments.
ex.resultPos: That leaves {{v}}, exactly the number in the Cash flow column.
ex.resultNeg: {{v}} is missing. You add this amount this year, as shown in the Cash flow column.
ex.monthly: That is roughly {{v}} a month on average.
ex.amortNote: The {{v}} repayment is not lost: with it you pay back your loan.
ex.rounding: If you add it up yourself, you get {{calc}}. The difference of {{diff}} only comes from each number in the table being rounded to whole euros on its own.

m.introTP: Cash flow means: money that comes in during a year minus money that goes out. The chart “{{chart}}” shows only the result for each year, the table below shows what it is made of. Each row is one calendar year for all apartments together. From left to right you see what comes in (rent), what goes out (costs, interest, repayment, taxes), what is added once (VAT refund), what is set aside for instalments and, on the far right, the result: the cash flow. A minus in front of a number means this amount goes out. A plus means it comes in. An empty cell means 0 €.
m.chartZero: A very flat green line right on zero means 0 €, in your plan {{inYears}}.
m.posFree: The rest is yours to use freely.
m.posRe: In the plan with reinvestment the surplus goes to your account (chart “{{chart}}” below). From there the model pays equity, meaning your own share of the purchase price, for additional apartments.
m.posReNoChart: In the plan with reinvestment the surplus goes to your account. From there the model pays equity, meaning your own share of the purchase price, for additional apartments.
m.posTP: Money set aside for instalments has already been deducted.
m.negTP: With instalments after the handover this can also happen in a year in which money is left over across the whole year, namely when the pot for instalments is empty in some months.
m.negRe: In the plan with reinvestment it comes from your account (chart “{{chart}}” below).
m.yearSale: In this last year all apartments are sold.
m.rentGrowth: From year to year the model assumes a rent increase of {{rg}} %.
m.rentSale: An apartment that is sold still counts until the end of December in its year of sale.
m.rentRe: Apartments that the model buys later on bring rent from their handover.
m.interestRe: On top of that comes the interest on refinancing, meaning new loans on finished apartments.
m.amortRe: The repayment of the refinancing loans is included here too.
m.taxDe: Your tax residence is Germany: Cyprus taxes the rental income first, and Germany credits the Cyprus tax against your German tax. The column shows the Cyprus tax plus the German tax, as far as any is left after the credit. If the apartments make a loss under German tax law, the model instead assumes a tax saving in Germany. If that saving is larger than the tax in Cyprus, the column shows a green plus.
m.taxCy: Your tax residence is Cyprus: the column shows the Cyprus income tax.
m.taxCyGesy: On top of that comes the GESY health contribution.
m.taxCySi: On top of that comes social insurance, because you let to holiday guests and count as self-employed for that.
m.taxFirma: You buy through a company: the column shows the corporation tax, meaning the tax on the company's profit, and the tax on the part of the profit the company pays out to you.
m.taxSale: Tax on a gain from selling is not here, but in the section “{{sec}}”.
m.vatSale: If you sell within ten years after the handover, you have to pay back part of a refund you received.
m.vatLate: In your plan at least one apartment is sold before its refund arrives. The model then counts this refund at the sale, reduced by the share for the years still missing until ten years after the handover.
m.vatRef: This is shown in the section “{{sec}}”.
m.vatNone: In your plan no refund arrives in this period, so the column stays empty.
m.toPayVat: The VAT refund is added to it.
m.toPayVatOut: A VAT refund that goes straight back to you does not go into the pot.
m.toPayRest: Instalments that are due are paid from the pot as far as your equity, meaning your own money, no longer covers them. Whatever is still missing comes from the loan. Before the pot starts and after the last instalment, every surplus is yours to use freely. Even while the pot exists, it only keeps what the coming instalments still need; the rest is yours to use freely. A month with a minus is also paid from the pot as long as there is money in it. If the pot then does not cover an instalment, the rest comes from the loan, even if money was free to use in other months of the year. The column shows how much of this year's result went into the pot: money that paid instalments this year or is in the pot at the end of the year for the next instalments. Money that was already in the pot from the previous year counts in the previous year. This money is not gone, it pays part of the purchase price for which you would otherwise need a bigger loan. But you cannot spend it freely, which is why it is deducted from the cash flow.
m.toPayPlus: A plus in this column means: more money flowed from the pot back into your cash flow this year than went in.
m.netCalc: The result of the row: rent minus costs, interest, repayment and taxes, plus VAT refund.
m.netCalcTP: The result of the row: rent minus costs, interest, repayment and taxes, plus VAT refund, minus “{{col}}”.
m.netGreen: Green means: this much is left over for you to use freely this year.
m.netGreenRe: Green means: this much is left over this year. In the plan with reinvestment it goes to your account (chart “{{chart}}” below).
m.netGreenReNoChart: Green means: this much is left over this year. In the plan with reinvestment it goes to your account.
m.netRe: Money from refinancing and equity for additional apartments are not here either, you see them in the chart “{{chart}}”.
m.ekLong: your equity, meaning your own money,
m.allZero: During the plan no apartment earns rent yet, and there are no costs or interest. That is why the cash flow is 0 € in every year.
m.negNone: In no year from {{first}} to {{last}} does a bar point down. According to the model, counted over the whole year, you never have to add money for the running payments.
m.negNoneSeason: If the model uses the seasonal calculation, single winter months can still have a minus.
m.negOne: Only in {{year}} does the bar point down: that year you add {{sum}} of your own money.
m.negMany: In {{n}} of {{total}} years the bar points down: {{years}}. In these years you add {{sum}} of your own money in total, the most in {{worstYear}} with {{worst}}.
m.negAll: In all {{total}} years the bar points down. You add {{sum}} of your own money in total, the most in {{worstYear}} with {{worst}}.
m.cumPos: Over all years together, {{cum}} is left over. That is where the blue line ends.
m.cumNeg: Over all years together, you put in {{abs}} more than the apartments bring in. That is why the blue line ends below zero, at {{cum}}.
m.scen: The same figure appears in the section “{{sec}}” in the column “{{col}}” as “{{row}}”.
m.saleNote: Proceeds from a sale are not included.
m.tpNote: The {{sum}} from the column “{{col}}” is not included either: this money paid instalments to the developer.
m.vatSum: This includes {{vat}} from the one-off VAT refund. Without it, it would be {{rest}}.
m.vatSumNeg: This includes {{vat}} from the one-off VAT refund. Without it, you would be {{abs}} in the red over all years.
m.first: {{year}} is the year of your first purchase contract. There is no rent and no running cost yet, which is why it shows 0 €. Payments towards the purchase price are not in this table. You pay them from your own money (equity) and, where that is not enough, with a loan. The table only shows the interest on such a loan.
m.buildOne: In {{year}} there is no rent yet, but already {{interest}} in interest. This is interest on credit you draw step by step before the handover, because instalments become due that your equity no longer covers.
m.buildMany: In the years {{years}} there is no rent yet, but already interest ({{list}}). This is interest on credit you draw step by step before the handover, because instalments become due that your equity no longer covers.
m.buildTax: In the model you get part of it back through German tax ({{list}}).
m.handover: In {{month}} {{year}} an apartment is handed over. Only {{months}} of {{year}} {{counts}} for this apartment: it brings in {{rent}} in rent that year.
m.handoverSeasonOne: If the model uses the seasonal calculation for this apartment, this month only counts with its seasonal share. Without the seasonal calculation, each month counts with one twelfth of the annual rent.
m.handoverSeasonDec: If the model uses the seasonal calculation for this apartment, this month only counts with its seasonal share, and a December then brings little. Without the seasonal calculation, each month counts with one twelfth of the annual rent.
m.handoverSeasonMany: If the model uses the seasonal calculation for this apartment, these months count with their seasonal share: summer months bring a lot, winter months little. Without the seasonal calculation, each month counts with one twelfth of the annual rent.
m.handoverNext: From {{year}} the model counts the whole year for it.
m.negAmort: {{InYears}} the cash flow is negative, but only because of the repayment: without it, {{left}}. So you pay part of the repayment from your own money there. That money is not gone, it reduces your loan.
m.leftMany: something would be left over in each of these years
m.negReal: {{InYears}} there would be a minus even without the repayment.
m.negRealHandoverOne: {{year}} is a handover year: one apartment only brings rent for part of that year.
m.negRealHandoverMany: {{years}} are handover years: in each, one apartment only brings rent for part of the year.
m.negRealBridge: Interest, on the other hand, already starts before the monthly loan payment, on credit you draw for instalments that are due.
m.taxPlus: {{InYears}} the Taxes column shows a plus. This is a tax saving in Germany: under German tax law the apartments make a loss {{inThese}}, because costs, interest and depreciation together are higher than the rent. Depreciation means the tax office lets you count part of the purchase price as a cost every year, even though no money is paid for it. The model assumes that this loss lowers your tax on your other income in Germany, by more than the tax due in Cyprus. Whether and how much this applies to you is something to check with your tax adviser.
m.levies: The Taxes column also contains levies that are not income tax: over all years together {{list}}. You can also find them in the section “{{sec}}”.
m.levySiNote: The model calculates social insurance for the whole year and on at least a fixed minimum income, even if rent only comes in for a few months.
m.levySiHigh: That is why in {{year}} it is even higher than that year's rent ({{rent}}).
m.vatRows: {{InYears}} a one-off VAT refund is added ({{list}}). {{look}} To see what the apartments bring in on an ongoing basis, subtract the refund: {{op}}.
m.lookOne: That is why this year looks especially good.
m.lookMany: That is why these years look especially good.
m.tpPos: In {{year}}, {{sub}} is left from {{src}} after costs, interest, repayment and taxes. Of this, {{tp}} goes into the pot for instalments. {{net}} remains free for you to use, which is the cash flow.
m.tpNegIntro: {{year}} looks contradictory at first sight: {{tp}} goes into the pot for instalments, and yet the cash flow is {{abs}} in the red. Both are true.
m.tpNegBalance: Across the whole year, {{sub}} is left from {{src}} after costs, interest, repayment and taxes. But {{tp}} goes into the pot, which is {{abs}} more than the whole year leaves over.
m.tpNegBalanceNeg: Across the whole year, {{subAbs}} is missing after costs, interest, repayment and taxes. Still, {{tp}} goes into the pot, so you add {{abs}} in total.
m.tpNegWhy: This fits together because the model calculates month by month here. A month with a minus is paid from the pot as long as there is money in it. If the pot is empty, you pay the minus yourself. The surpluses of the other months go into the pot as far as the next instalments need them. What stays there does not make up for the minus you paid yourself.
m.tpNegEmpty: At the start of {{year}} the pot was empty.
m.tpNegStart: The pot has only existed since {{month}} {{startYear}}, the handover of the apartment for which instalments are still due afterwards.
m.tpNegStartBuy: The pot has only existed since {{month}} {{startYear}}, the purchase of the already finished apartment for which instalments are still due afterwards.
m.tpNegPrevFree: What was left over in {{prevYear}} ({{prevNet}}) was free to use and is already counted as cash flow in the {{prevYear}} row.
m.tpNegSeason: If the model uses the seasonal calculation, the winter months bring little rent, while costs, interest, repayment and taxes continue evenly. Months with a minus then fall mainly in winter, at the beginning and at the end of the year.
m.tpNegSeasonEmpty: With the seasonal calculation, the weak winter months fall at the beginning of {{year}}, when the pot was still empty. You then add their minus yourself.
m.potPaid: In {{year}} instalments totalling {{paid}} were paid from the pot.
m.potPaidPrev: In {{year}} instalments totalling {{paid}} were paid from the pot, {{prev}} of it from the previous year.
m.potEnd: At the end of the year {{end}} is in the pot for the next instalments.
m.credit: Which instalment is paid from where is shown in the section “{{sec}}”.
m.rounding: If you add up the columns yourself, you get {{calc}} instead of {{sub}}. The difference only comes from rounding.
m.tpPlus: {{InYears}} the column “{{col}}” shows a plus: more money flowed from the pot back into your cash flow than went in, for example because it covered months with a minus or was no longer needed for instalments.
m.saleRun: The model calculates as if you sell at the end of the year: rent and costs run until the end of December, and the row only shows this running part.
m.saleRunHand: The model calculates as if you sell at the end of the year: rent and costs run until the end of December (for an apartment handed over only this year, from the handover). The row only shows this running part.
m.saleZero: There is no rent yet this year, which is why the row shows 0 €.
m.saleNoRent: There is no rent yet this year. The row only shows the other running payments until the end of December.
m.saleResult: What the sale itself brings is shown in the section “{{sec}}”: after {{ded}}, {{net}} is left there.
m.saleVatOpen: This already includes the VAT refund still outstanding, reduced by the share for the years still missing until ten years after the handover.
m.dedBase: the remaining loan, selling costs and taxes
m.dedVat: the remaining loan, selling costs, repayment of VAT refund and taxes
m.saleEquity: On top of that comes {{v}} of equity that was reserved for later instalments and is no longer needed.
m.saleRe: {{InYears}} the model sells one or more apartments. A sold apartment still counts until the end of December in its year of sale. The proceeds are not in this table, they go to your account (chart “{{chart}}” below).
m.keysBase: the first, the 5th, the 10th and the last year
m.keysRe: the first, the 5th, the 10th and the last year, plus years in which the model buys an additional apartment or sells one
m.hiddenOne: The table leaves out years without rent unless they are key years{{view}}. Key years are {{keys}}. That is why {{year}} is missing. The chart still includes it, its cash flow: {{sum}}.
m.hiddenMany: The table leaves out years without rent unless they are key years{{view}}. Key years are {{keys}}. That is why {{years}} are missing. The chart still includes them, their cash flow together: {{sum}}.
m.hiddenView: (as long as only the key years are shown)
m.cut: The table first shows 12 years, up to {{lastShown}}. To see all years up to {{last}}, tap or click “{{more}}” further up in the section “{{sec}}”. The chart shows all years.
m.cutFixed: The table only shows the first 12 years, up to {{lastShown}}. The chart shows all years up to {{last}}.
m.cutNeg: Note: {{InYears}} the cash flow is negative.

pitfalls.notProfit: Cash flow is not profit. The repayment is deducted, even though it reduces your loan and so more of the apartment belongs to you. A possible increase in value of the apartments is not in the table at all. A small or negative cash flow therefore does not automatically mean you are losing wealth.
pitfalls.vatOnce: A tall bar is not automatically a good year. The VAT refund comes only once per apartment. Whether the apartments carry themselves on an ongoing basis, you see in the years without a refund.
pitfalls.line: The blue line is neither return nor profit. It only adds up the money that is left over or missing each year. Purchase price, increase in value and sale proceeds are not included.
pitfalls.purchase: Instalments to the developer are not repayment. What you pay towards the purchase price, from equity or with a loan, is not in the table. You only see the interest on that loan.
pitfalls.purchaseTP: Instalments to the developer are not repayment. What you pay towards the purchase price, from equity or with a loan, is not in the table. You only see the interest on that loan. Only the part paid by the apartments' surpluses appears in the column “{{col}}”.
pitfalls.taxPlus: A plus in the Taxes column is a tax saving in Germany under the model's assumptions, not a payment from Cyprus.
pitfalls.saleYear: The year of sale only shows the running part. Sale proceeds, paying back the remaining loan and tax on the sale are shown in the section “{{sec}}”.
pitfalls.saleYearRe: A year of sale only shows the running part. The proceeds from the sale go to your account and are not in the table.
pitfalls.tpMinus: A negative cash flow despite large amounts “{{col}}” is not a calculation error. The model calculates month by month: surpluses are set aside for the next instalments and are not offset against the minus of a month in which the pot was empty.
pitfalls.notAllYears: The table does not show every year. The chart above always shows all years.
pitfalls.notAllYearsRe: As long as only the key years are shown, the table does not show every year. The chart above always shows all years.
pitfalls.scale: The line and the bars use the same euro numbers on the left. If the line rises very high, the bars look small, even when several thousand euros are involved.
pitfalls.rounding: Each number is rounded to whole euros on its own. If you add up a row or the bars yourself, the result can differ by a few euros.
pitfalls.model: All numbers are a model calculation with assumed rents, costs, interest and taxes. The real values can differ, up or down.

liquidity.heading: How to read the “{{chart}}” chart
liquidity.intro: Liquidity means money you can use right away. The blue line shows how much of it is in your account in the model at the end of each year. The account starts with the part of your starting capital that does not go into the first purchases. This chart only exists in the plan with reinvestment, because there money flows from the account into additional apartments. The numbers on the left are euros: k means thousand, Mio means million. On a computer, move the mouse over a year to see the exact balance.

cash.label: Liquidity
cash.text: The blue line, your account balance in the model at the end of the year. It rises with a positive cash flow from the table above, with money from refinancing and with proceeds from sales. Refinancing means a new loan on a finished apartment. It brings money into the account, but increases your debt. The balance falls with a negative cash flow and with equity, meaning your own share of the purchase price, and purchase costs for additional apartments, including instalments for an apartment that is still being built. The dot at the end of the line marks the last balance.

reserve.label: Reserve
reserve.text: The dashed line at {{reserve}}. This is the minimum reserve from your plan: money that should always stay in the account as a cushion for the unexpected, for example a repair or a month without guests. The model only buys an additional apartment if, by its calculation, the reserve is kept in the year of purchase and in the years after.

warn.label: Note on liquidity
warn.text: This box appears because the blue line is below {{level}} in at least one year.

ex.main: The year {{year}}: at the end of {{prev}} there is {{prevCash}} in the account. In {{year}} nothing flows into or out of the account apart from the cash flow: no purchase, no refinancing, no sale. {{cf}} So at the end of {{year}} there is {{cash}} in the account.
ex.pos: The {{year}} cash flow from the table above adds {{v}}.
ex.neg: The {{year}} cash flow from the table above is negative: you add {{v}}, and this money comes from this account.

m.cashInvestor: On top of that comes the money you pay in every month according to your plan ({{v}} a month).
m.reserve0: The dashed line is at 0 €, because you have not set a minimum reserve. A minimum reserve would be money that should always stay in the account as a cushion for the unexpected. Without it, the model only buys an additional apartment if, by its calculation, the account does not fall below 0 € in the year of purchase and in the years after.
m.warnBuy: In those years you would need extra money in the model, or an additional purchase would have to come later.
m.warnNoBuy: In those years you would need extra money in the model. The box also mentions a later purchase as a way out. That does not help here, because the model buys no additional apartment by the end of {{to}}.
m.warnNoBuyAll: In those years you would need extra money in the model. The box also mentions a later purchase as a way out. That does not help here, because the model buys no additional apartment in your plan.
m.warnSingle: The box only means the year {{from}}.
m.warnGaps: The box names the period from the first to the last of these years. In between there are years in which the line is not below {{level}}.
m.ok: The line is not below the reserve of {{reserve}} in any year. So in the model the money is enough every year without touching this cushion.
m.ok0: The line does not fall below 0 € in any year. So in the model the money is enough every year. But no cushion for the unexpected is planned.
m.belowOne: In {{year}} the line is below the reserve of {{reserve}}, at {{lowest}}.
m.below: {{InYears}} the line is below the reserve of {{reserve}}, at its lowest in {{lowYear}} with {{lowest}}.
m.belowOne0: In {{year}} the line falls below 0 €, to {{lowest}}.
m.below0: {{InYears}} the line is below 0 €, at its lowest in {{lowYear}} with {{lowest}}.
m.belowPos: Your account is not in the red, but the cushion is smaller than planned.
m.belowNeg: At its lowest point the account would even be {{abs}} in the red. You would then have to put in at least this much extra money.
m.belowNeg0: The account would then be in the red. You would have to put in at least {{abs}} extra.
m.cause: The reason here is not a purchase but the negative cash flow of {{year}} ({{net}}).
m.causeFirst: For {{year}}, the first of these years, the reason is not a purchase but the negative cash flow of that year ({{net}}).
m.move: In {{year}} {{move}}. The cash flow of that year is {{net}}.
m.moveOut: The difference of {{diff}} is money that went from the account into additional apartments: equity and purchase costs{{offset}}.
m.moveOutBuild: The difference of {{diff}} is money that went from the account into additional apartments: instalments and purchase costs for an apartment the model bought earlier and that is still being built{{offset}}.
m.moveMinusEq: , after deducting equity for additional apartments
m.moveSec: What is bought, refinanced or sold that year is shown in the section “{{sec}}”.
m.tail: From {{year}} the line falls year by year until the end of the plan. In these years the cash flow is negative, and the money for it comes from this account.
m.end: At the end of the plan, in {{year}}, there is {{cash}} in the account in the model. This money counts towards your net worth.
m.endNeg: At the end of the plan, in {{year}}, the account would be {{abs}} in the red in the model. This amount reduces your net worth.

pitfalls.refi: More money in the account does not mean more profit. Money from refinancing is a new loan: it fills the account, but increases your debt.
pitfalls.equity: If the line falls because equity flows into an additional apartment, the money is not gone. It is now in that apartment.
pitfalls.yearEnd: The line shows the balance at the end of the year. The model does not calculate here what happens within a year.
pitfalls.reserve: The reserve is a target from your plan, not a bank requirement.
pitfalls.rounding: In years without a purchase, refinancing or sale, the previous year's balance plus the cash flow gives the new balance. If you check this yourself, it can differ by 1 € due to rounding.
pitfalls.roundingNarrow: In years without a purchase, refinancing or sale, in which no instalment and no purchase costs for an additionally bought apartment are due either and you pay in nothing extra, the previous year's balance plus the cash flow gives the new balance (up to 1 € rounding). In the other years equity also flows out or money flows in.
pitfalls.cut: The table above first shows only 12 years, the line shows all years. If the line falls at the end, use “{{more}}” to see the late years in the table.

creditPath.heading: How to read the boxes and the instalment table
creditPath.intro: This section shows how the purchase prices of your apartments are paid step by step, and from when you need money from the bank. Each row of the table is one purchase price instalment, a payment towards the price of an apartment, usually to the developer (the company that builds and sells it). The rows are in the order the instalments fall due. Payments for the same apartment in the same month share one row. From left to right you read: when, what for, how much, and where the money comes from. An empty cell means nothing comes from that source. The table runs to the end of the last year of your plan; for an apartment sold earlier, to the end of the year it is sold. The three boxes above sum everything up for all apartments together. Equity here means the part of your starting capital that goes into the purchase prices.

eqUntil.label: Equity lasts until
eqUntil.text: The month of the last instalment{{fin}} that still gets money from your equity before a loan is needed for the first time. The row in which a loan is needed for the first time does not count here, even if it still gets some equity.

eqUntilAll.label: Equity lasts until
eqUntilAll.text: It says “{{v}}”: your equity pays every instalment in the table in full.

eqUntilFirst.label: Equity lasts until
eqUntilFirst.text: It says “{{v}}”: your equity is not even enough for the whole first instalment.

from.label: Loan needed from
from.text: The month in which, for the first time, an instalment{{fin}} can no longer be paid in full from your own money. From then on you need money from the bank, in other words a loan. This row is highlighted in the table, and the box is marked in coral.

fromNone.label: Loan needed from
fromNone.text: It says “{{v}}”: your equity pays all instalments in the table. You don't need a bank for the purchase prices.

fromNoneCash.label: Loan needed from
fromNoneCash.text: It says “{{v}}” because only your apartments with bank financing count in this box. A loan for a cash purchase is not counted here.

fromNoneRent.label: Loan needed from
fromNoneRent.text: It says “{{v}}”: whatever your equity doesn't pay is covered by the surplus from rent. No loan is needed for the purchase prices.

fromNoneSurplus.label: Loan needed from
fromNoneSurplus.text: It says “{{v}}”: whatever your equity doesn't pay is covered by the surplus from rent and the VAT refund. No loan is needed for the purchase prices.

total.label: Total loan
total.text: All amounts in the “Loan” column added up. This is how much the bank lends you in total for purchase instalments up to the end of the table. Interest and purchase costs are not included, and later repayments are not deducted.

date.label: Due
date.text: Month and year in which the instalment is due. Construction instalments fall due when a construction stage is finished, so their months are estimates and can move.

rate.label: Instalment
rate.text: On top you see the apartment, below it the payment. This can be a share at contract signing, a finished construction stage, the share at handover (when you get the keys and letting starts) or an instalment after handover, which you pay to the developer only after you have the keys. The payment names are currently shown in German, for example “bei Vertrag” (at contract), “bei Übergabe” (at handover) or “Rate 1/8 nach Übergabe” (instalment 1 of 8 after handover). “Reservierung” is a reservation deposit that counts towards the price. Percentages refer to the apartment's total price. If two payments are joined with “+”, they fall due in the same month and are added together. If the handover payment says “abzüglich Reservierung” (minus reservation), the reservation is deducted there again.

amount.label: Amount
amount.text: How much of the price is due with this instalment, including VAT and, if chosen, a share of the furniture package. Purchase costs and interest are not included. All amounts of one apartment add up to its total price, as far as its instalments are in the table.

equity.label: from equity
equity.text: The part of the instalment paid from your equity. It is used in date order, across all apartments, until it is used up.

surplus.label: from rent/VAT
surplus.text: The part of the instalment paid by the surplus of your let apartments. Surplus means rent minus management, running costs, interest, repayments and taxes, plus the VAT refund. The VAT refund means: with short-term letting to holiday guests you get the VAT on the apartment price back, fully or partly, in the model about 18 months after handover. The surplus is saved up and pays instalments before a loan is needed. Green means this money comes from your income.

surplusRent.label: from rent
surplusRent.text: The part of the instalment paid by the surplus of your let apartments. Surplus means the rent minus management, running costs, interest, repayments and taxes. It is saved up and pays instalments before a loan is needed. Green means this money comes from your income.

credit.label: Loan
credit.text: The part of the instalment the bank pays because the rest of the money isn't enough. You draw the loan in stages as the instalments fall due. Until a loan's fixed monthly payment starts, you only pay interest on it. The number is orange and bold so you spot it right away.

cumul.label: Loan total
cumul.text: All loan amounts from the top down to this row added up. The number only grows and never falls, because repayments are not deducted here. The last row shows the same number as the “Total loan” box.

cumulNone.label: Loan total
cumulNone.text: All loan amounts from the top down to this row added up. As long as no loan is needed, the column stays empty.

interest.label: plus interest
interest.text: Only for instalments after handover: the developer charges interest on the part of the price that is still open. You pay it on top of the amount. For these instalments of one apartment, amount plus interest is about the same each time. Bank interest is not in this column.

eqUntilNoCredit.label: Equity lasts until
eqUntilNoCredit.text: The month of the last instalment{{fin}} that still gets money from your equity. Later instalments{{fin}} are paid by the surplus from {{quelle}}.

eqUntilNoCreditLast.label: Equity lasts until
