eqUntilNoCreditLast.text: The month of the last instalment{{fin}} that still gets money from your equity.

eqUntilAllCash.label: Equity lasts until
eqUntilAllCash.text: It says “{{v}}”: your equity pays every instalment of your apartments with bank financing in full. The table only shows a loan for a cash purchase.

eqUntilFirstCash.label: Equity lasts until
eqUntilFirstCash.text: It says “{{v}}”: after the part reserved for cash purchases, your equity is not even enough for the whole first instalment of your apartments with bank financing.

fromMulti.label: Loan needed from
fromMulti.text: The month in which, for the first time, an instalment{{fin}} can no longer be paid in full from your own money. From then on you need money from the bank, in other words a loan. All rows of this month that show a loan are highlighted in the table, and the box is marked in coral.

fromNoneRentCash.label: Loan needed from
fromNoneRentCash.text: It says “{{v}}”: whatever your equity doesn't pay for your apartments with bank financing is covered by the surplus from rent. No loan is needed for their purchase prices. A loan for a cash purchase is not counted in this box.

fromNoneSurplusCash.label: Loan needed from
fromNoneSurplusCash.text: It says “{{v}}”: whatever your equity doesn't pay for your apartments with bank financing is covered by the surplus from rent and the VAT refund. No loan is needed for their purchase prices. A loan for a cash purchase is not counted in this box.

ex.firstEq: Up to and including {{eqBis}}, all instalments{{fin}} due are paid without a loan.
ex.firstEqSame: In {{kreditAb}}, one instalment{{fin}} still gets money from your equity first.
ex.firstEqNone: Your equity is not even enough for the whole first instalment.
ex.firstEqNoneCash: After the part reserved for cash purchases, your equity is not even enough for the whole first instalment of your apartments with bank financing.
ex.row: In {{kreditAb}}, an instalment of {{betrag}} is due, highlighted in the table.
ex.rowMulti: In {{kreditAb}}, an instalment of {{betrag}} is due, the first highlighted row.
ex.rowSame: After that, an instalment of {{betrag}} is due in the same month, highlighted in the table.
ex.eqOnly: Your equity {{noch}}pays {{ausEk}} of it. The missing {{kredit}} is your first loan.
ex.eqSur: Of this, {{ausEk}} {{noch}}comes from your equity and {{ausMiete}} from {{quelle}}. The missing {{kredit}} is your first loan.
ex.surOnly: Of this, {{ausMiete}} comes from {{quelle}}. The missing {{kredit}} is your first loan.
ex.noneLeft: No equity is left for this instalment. The whole instalment comes as a loan from the bank, and that is your first loan.
ex.rest: With the further loan amounts up to the end of the table, the total comes to {{gesamt}}. This number is shown in the “Total loan” box and in the last row under “Loan total”.
ex.restNone: Your plan needs no further loans for the purchase prices.
ex.last: In the last row ({{faellig}}), {{betrag}} is due: {{teile}}.{{zins}}
ex.lastOne: In the last row ({{faellig}}), {{betrag}} is due. {{teil}}.{{zins}}
ex.oneEq: All of it comes from your equity
ex.oneCredit: All of it comes as a loan from the bank
ex.lastInterest: On top, you pay {{zinsen}} interest to the developer.
ex.noCredit: All {{n}} instalments add up to {{summe}}. Your equity pays all of them, the last one in {{letzte}}. That is why the “Loan” column stays empty and the “Total loan” box shows {{null}}.
ex.noCredit2: Both instalments add up to {{summe}}. Your equity pays both of them, the last one in {{letzte}}. That is why the “Loan” column stays empty and the “Total loan” box shows {{null}}.
ex.noCredit1: The only instalment, {{summe}} in {{letzte}}, is paid entirely from your equity. That is why the “Loan” column stays empty and the “Total loan” box shows {{null}}.

m.need: For you this means: before {{kreditAb}} you need no loan for the purchase prices. Your bank financing should be in place by then, because from that month your own money is no longer enough for the instalments.
m.needEarly: For you this means: from {{kreditAb}} you need a loan for your apartments with bank financing. Your bank financing should be in place by then.
m.same: Several instalments are due in {{kreditAb}}. The first one still gets money from your equity, but there is not enough for the next one. So your bank financing should already be in place in that month.
m.start: You need the loan right from the first instalment, in {{kreditAb}}. So your bank financing should already be in place at that point.
m.noneEq: Your equity pays all purchase instalments in the table. In this plan you need no loan for the purchase prices.
m.noneSurplusVat: Whatever your equity doesn't cover is paid by the surplus from rent and the VAT refund. Your plan needs no loan for the purchase prices. If rent or the refund turn out lower than assumed, this can change.
m.noneSurplusRent: Whatever your equity doesn't cover is paid by the surplus from rent. Your plan needs no loan for the purchase prices. If the rent turns out lower than assumed, this can change.
m.cashOnlyCredit: The only loan here is for a cash purchase where the reserved equity is not quite enough. That is why the “Loan needed from” box shows no month, even though “Total loan” shows {{gesamt}}.
m.cashRes: Apartments you buy without a bank loan (cash purchase) are not counted for “Equity lasts until” and “Loan needed from”. A fixed part of your equity is reserved for them.
m.reinvest: Because your plan reinvests money that becomes free, a reserve of {{reserve}} stays in your account, and the purchase costs are deducted first. That is why {{ek}} of your starting capital is planned for the purchase prices. Loans for later purchases and refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) are not included in “Total loan”.
m.reinvestNoReserve: Because your plan reinvests money that becomes free, the purchase costs are deducted from your starting capital first. That is why {{ek}} of your starting capital is planned for the purchase prices. Loans for later purchases and refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) are not included in “Total loan”.
m.surplus: From {{ab}}, the surplus from {{quelle}} pays part of the instalments, {{summe}} in total. This money is set aside until each instalment is due, so you can't use it freely in the meantime. In the table in the section “{{s5}}” you see it in the column “{{toPay}}”.
m.interest: For the instalments after handover, the developer charges interest on the part of the price that is still open, {{summe}} in total. It comes on top of the amounts and is included in the table in the section “{{s5}}” in the column “{{zinsen}}”.
m.again: After the first loan there are instalments again that need no new loan at all. By then, enough surplus from {{quelle}} has built up.
m.vatReturned1: For one apartment, the VAT refund goes straight back to you. It therefore pays no instalments, so more loan may be needed.
m.vatReturnedN: For {{n}} apartments, the VAT refund goes straight back to you. It therefore pays no instalments, so more loan may be needed.
m.openRest: Instalments that would only fall due after the end of your plan are not in this table. You find them on the apartment's card under {{labels}}.
m.overEquity: This table shows more equity ({{ek}}) than your starting capital of {{start}} provides. The reason: here the strategy always pays apartments without a bank loan (cash purchase) at their full price from equity. You would have to provide the difference on top.
m.startCash: You need the loan right from the first instalment of your apartments with bank financing, in {{kreditAb}}. So your bank financing should already be in place at that point.
m.cashCredit1: For an apartment without “{{darlehen}}” on its card, the instalment table still shows a loan, {{kredit}} in total. The reason: the table spreads your equity over all apartments by date only, and earlier instalments have already used it up. On its card, this apartment is paid entirely from equity.
m.cashCreditN: For {{n}} apartments without “{{darlehen}}” on their cards, the instalment table still shows a loan, {{kredit}} in total. The reason: the table spreads your equity over all apartments by date only, and earlier instalments have already used it up. On their cards, these apartments are paid entirely from equity.
m.reinvestOver: Because your plan reinvests money that becomes free, a reserve of {{reserve}} stays in your account, and the purchase costs are deducted from your starting capital first. Loans for later purchases and refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) are not included in “Total loan”.
m.reinvestOverNoReserve: Because your plan reinvests money that becomes free, the purchase costs are deducted from your starting capital first. Loans for later purchases and refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) are not included in “Total loan”.
m.reinvestPart: Because your plan reinvests money that becomes free, a reserve of {{reserve}} stays in your account, and the purchase costs are deducted from your starting capital first. {{ek}} of your starting capital is planned for the purchase prices. Loans for later purchases and refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) are not included in “Total loan”.
m.reinvestPartNoReserve: Because your plan reinvests money that becomes free, the purchase costs are deducted from your starting capital first. {{ek}} of your starting capital is planned for the purchase prices. Loans for later purchases and refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) are not included in “Total loan”.

pitfalls.notDebt: “Total loan” is not what you owe on a given day but the sum of all amounts drawn. Once the monthly payments start, you keep paying part of it back. How high your debt is year by year is shown in the section “{{s6}}”.
pitfalls.interest: Interest is not part of “Total loan”. It is shown year by year in the table in the section “{{s5}}” in the column “{{zinsen}}”.
pitfalls.costs: The purchase costs (in the model 1 percent of the apartment price including VAT, without furniture) are not in this table. They come on top of the equity shown here.
pitfalls.shift: The months of the construction instalments depend on construction progress. If building goes faster or slower, the instalments move, and so do the months in the boxes.
pitfalls.devInterest: The column “plus interest” shows only the developer's interest. The bank's interest on the loan drawn is in the column “{{zinsen}}” in the section “{{s5}}”.
pitfalls.round: Every number is rounded to whole euros. That is why a row can be off by 1 € and a column total by a few euros.
pitfalls.model: This is a model calculation, not a loan commitment from a bank.
pitfalls.costsExtra: The purchase costs (in the model 1 percent of the apartment price including VAT, without furniture) are not in this table. You pay them on top of your starting capital.
pitfalls.sameMonth: Within the same month, the order of the apartments is fixed technically. Which apartment gets the last bit of equity therefore says nothing about the apartment.

creditPath.fin: of your apartments with bank financing

ueb.def: Surplus means rent minus management, running costs, interest, repayments and taxes.

vat.def: The VAT refund is the VAT on the apartment price that you get back, fully or partly, with short-term letting.

bt.def: The developer is the company that builds and sells the apartment.

abg.def: Drawn means already paid out by the bank.

rest.known: part of a loan you have not yet paid back
rest.def: The remaining debt is the part of a loan you have not yet paid back.

nk.def: Purchase costs are costs that come on top of the price when you buy.

refi.def: A refinancing is an additional loan on an apartment that has already been handed over.

reinv.known: reinvests money that becomes free|[Rr]einvestment means
reinv.def: Reinvestment means the model puts money that becomes free back into further apartments.

erl.def: The proceeds are the money the sale brings in.

loans.heading: How to read the bank loans
loans.intro: The loan amounts from the instalment table turn into fixed bank loans. A bank loan is money the bank lends you for many years, which you pay back in fixed monthly payments. Each row is one apartment with a loan, sorted by the month in which the monthly payment starts. You see how big the loan is, from when the monthly payment runs and how high it is.

apt.label: Apartment
apt.text: The apartment the loan is for.

loan.label: Loan
loan.text: How much the bank lends you for this apartment, counted at the start. With every monthly payment the debt gets smaller; this is the starting amount. The same number is on the apartment's card in the section “{{s7}}”.

start.label: Monthly payment from
start.text: From this month you pay the fixed monthly payment to the bank. Normally this is the month of handover. If you still pay instalments to the developer after handover, it only starts in the month of the last of those instalments. Before that you only pay interest on the loan already drawn.

monthly.label: Monthly payment
monthly.text: The fixed amount you pay the bank every month. It contains interest (the price of borrowing) and repayment. At the start the interest share is large; later the repayment share grows. It is calculated with the assumed interest rate and the assumed term.

open.label: open, interest only
open.text: You buy this apartment without a bank loan (cash purchase), but your equity is not quite enough for the price. The gap runs as a loan on which you only pay interest. In the model there is no monthly payment with repayment for it. The loan is paid off at the sale or remains as debt at the end.

sold.label: repaid from the sale proceeds
sold.text: The apartment is sold before the monthly payment would start. The loan drawn until then is paid back from the sale proceeds, meaning the money the sale brings in. That is why no monthly payment is shown.

after.label: after the period ({{d}})
after.text: The monthly payment would only start after the end of your plan, in the month in brackets. Until then you only pay interest on the loan drawn. The amount is the loan drawn by the end of your plan.

monthly0.label: Monthly payment
monthly0.text: The fixed amount you pay the bank every month. At 0 % interest it is pure repayment, spread over the assumed term.

ex.firstRate: In the first row with a monthly payment
ex.main: {{welche}}, the bank lends you {{darlehen}} for the apartment. From {{start}} you pay {{rate}} for it every month. This contains interest and repayment, calculated with {{zins}} % interest per year and a term of {{laufzeit}}.
ex.paidOff: After this term the loan is fully paid back on paper.
ex.paidOffSale: After this term the loan would be fully paid back on paper. Because the apartment is sold as early as {{jahr}} in your plan, the debt still open then is repaid from the sale proceeds.
ex.early: According to the instalment table, you already need the first loan from {{kreditAb}}, before this monthly payment starts. Until a monthly payment starts, you only pay interest on the loan drawn.
ex.sum: All loans together add up to {{summe}}, exactly the number in the “Total loan” box.
ex.sumOne: That is also the number in the “Total loan” box.
ex.main0: {{welche}}, the bank lends you {{darlehen}} for the apartment. From {{start}} you pay {{rate}} for it every month. At 0 % interest the monthly payment is pure repayment, spread over a term of {{laufzeit}}.
ex.mainSoldBefore: {{welche}} there is a loan of {{darlehen}} for the apartment, with a monthly payment of {{rate}} from {{start}}, calculated with {{zins}} % interest per year and a term of {{laufzeit}}. Because the apartment is already sold in {{jahr}} in your plan, before that month, you never pay this monthly payment in the plan.
ex.mainSoldBefore0: {{welche}} there is a loan of {{darlehen}} for the apartment, with a monthly payment of {{rate}} from {{start}}. At 0 % interest it is pure repayment, spread over a term of {{laufzeit}}. Because the apartment is already sold in {{jahr}} in your plan, before that month, you never pay this monthly payment in the plan.
ex.early0: According to the instalment table, you already need the first loan from {{kreditAb}}, before this monthly payment starts. At 0 % interest, the loan drawn costs you nothing until then.

m.together: From {{ab}}, all {{n}} monthly payments run at the same time. For these loans you then pay the bank {{summe}} a month in total. Management, running costs and taxes come on top. Whether the rent covers all of this is shown in the table in the section “{{s5}}”.
m.together2: From {{ab}}, both monthly payments run at the same time. For these loans you then pay the bank {{summe}} a month in total. Management, running costs and taxes come on top. Whether the rent covers all of this is shown in the table in the section “{{s5}}”.
m.matchExact: Each loan is exactly the loan amount that adds up for this apartment in the instalment table.
m.matchRound1: Each loan is the loan amount that adds up for this apartment in the instalment table. If you add up the cells yourself, rounding can make it differ by 1 €.
m.matchRound: Each loan is the loan amount that adds up for this apartment in the instalment table. If you add up the cells yourself, rounding can make it differ by a few euros.
m.open1: For an apartment bought in cash, your equity is not quite enough. {{betrag}} runs there as a loan with interest only, without repayment.
m.openN: For {{n}} apartments bought in cash, your equity is not quite enough. {{betrag}} in total runs there as a loan with interest only, without repayment.
m.sold1: One apartment is sold before its monthly payment starts. The {{betrag}} of loan drawn until then is paid back from the sale proceeds. Until the sale, only interest is charged on it.
m.soldN: {{n}} apartments are sold before their monthly payment starts. The {{betrag}} of loan drawn until then is paid back from the sale proceeds. Until the sale, only interest is charged on it.
m.after: For one apartment the monthly payment only starts after the end of your plan, in {{start}}. By then {{betrag}} of loan has been drawn, on which you only pay interest.

pitfalls.costs: The monthly payment is not everything an apartment costs per month. Management, running costs and taxes come on top.
pitfalls.start: “Loan” is the starting amount. How high your debt is at the end is shown in the section “{{s6}}” under “{{fDebt}}”.
pitfalls.interest: Interest charged before the monthly payment starts is not shown here but in the column “{{zinsen}}” in the section “{{s5}}”.
pitfalls.assume: Interest rate and term are assumptions of the calculation, not an offer from a bank.
pitfalls.pooled: In the instalment table your equity is used in date order across all apartments. How much loan appears there for which apartment can therefore differ from this table. The total is the same.
pitfalls.mismatch: The loans here add up to {{summe}}, while the “Total loan” box shows {{gesamt}}.
pitfalls.mismatchSold: The loans here add up to {{summe}}, while the “Total loan” box shows {{gesamt}}. The difference arises because an apartment is sold before its handover: this table still shows its planned loan with a monthly payment, while its later instalments are missing from the instalment table.
pitfalls.mismatchCash: The loans here add up to {{summe}}, while the “Total loan” box shows {{gesamt}}. One reason: the instalment table spreads your equity by date only, also onto apartments without a loan. They therefore show a loan there that has no row here.
pitfalls.mismatchCut: One reason: instalments that only fall due after the end of your plan are missing from the instalment table.
pitfalls.mismatchCutAlso: Also, instalments that only fall due after the end of your plan are missing from the instalment table.

timeline.heading: How to read the timeline
timeline.intro: The timeline shows the important events of your plan in order, year by year. Each entry starts with the year (in bold) and the event, with the numbers below. The entries themselves currently appear in German: “Kauf” means purchase, “Übergabe” handover, “Refinanzierung” refinancing and “Verkauf” sale.
timeline.dots: The dot on the left shows the type: {{list}}.

dot.grey: grey for purchase and handover of your apartments
dot.blue: blue for a further purchase planned by the model

buy.label: Kauf …
buy.text: Grey dot: you sign the purchase contract for one of your apartments. “gesamt” is the total price including VAT and, if chosen, the furniture package. “davon … Eigenkapital” is your own money for this apartment, including purchase costs. The same numbers are on its card under “Total price” and “of which equity”.

buyModel.label: Kauf …
buyModel.text: Blue dot: a further purchase that the model plans itself. It pays the equity part with reused money, such as surpluses, VAT refunds, refinancing or sale proceeds, and the rest with a bank loan. This apartment is a placeholder, not one that has already been chosen.

plan.label: Zahlungsplan
plan.text: “Payment plan”: when which part of the price is due: at contract, by construction progress, at handover and, if applicable, in instalments after handover, then with the developer's interest rate.

planTable.label: Zahlungsplan
planTable.text: “Payment plan”: when which part of the price is due: at contract, by construction progress, at handover and, if applicable, in instalments after handover, then with the developer's interest rate. You see the individual instalments further down in the section “{{credTitle}}”, in the instalment table.

handover.label: Übergabe …
handover.text: You get the keys. From this month the model counts rent. The exact months are on the apartment cards.

rentOnly.label: Ab hier fließt Miete
rentOnly.text: “Rent flows from here”: from handover there is rental income. If only this sentence is shown, there is no bank loan for this apartment.

rentLoan.label: Ab hier fließt Miete, und Zins und Tilgung laufen
rentLoan.text: “Rent flows from here, and interest and repayment run”: from handover there is rent, and from then on you also pay the fixed monthly payment to the bank, made up of interest and repayment.

after.label: … an den Bauträger, zuzüglich … Zinsen
after.text: “… to the developer, plus … interest”: part of the price is paid to the developer in instalments only after handover. The developer charges interest on the part still open, which comes on top of the instalments. Only instalments within your plan are counted.

from.label: Davon kommen …
from.text: “Of this, … comes from”: where the money for exactly these instalments after handover comes from: from the rent surplus (with the VAT refund, if any), from your equity or from the bank. Only sources that contribute are named. Together they add up, apart from rounding, to the instalment amount before, without the interest.

rest.label: Die restlichen …
rest.text: “The remaining …”: instalments to the developer that only fall due after the end of your plan. If your plan ends with a sale, they are paid from the sale proceeds.

loanFrom.label: Das Bankdarlehen läuft ab …
loanFrom.text: “The bank loan runs from …”: from this month you pay the fixed monthly payment to the bank. Before that you only pay interest on the loan already drawn.

loanFromTable.label: Das Bankdarlehen läuft ab …
loanFromTable.text: “The bank loan runs from …”: from this month you pay the fixed monthly payment to the bank. Before that you only pay interest on the loan already drawn. The same month is shown further down in the box “{{credLoans}}”.

cashGap.label: Für den Barkauf fehlen …
cashGap.text: “For the cash purchase … is missing”: you buy this apartment without a bank loan, but your equity is not quite enough. The gap runs as a loan on which you only pay interest.

refi.label: Refinanzierung
refi.text: Green dot: the bank lends you additional money on an apartment that has already been handed over. This works if the apartment is worth enough more than the debt still on it. “werden wieder verfügbar” (become available again) means the money goes into your account and can be used for further purchases. But it is a new loan, and your debt rises by this amount.

sale.label: Verkauf …
sale.text: Coral dot: one apartment is sold on its own. The number is what reaches you after the loan is paid off and selling costs, any repayment of the VAT refund and taxes are paid.

ex.main: One of your apartments is bought in {{kauf}} and handed over in {{uebergabe}}, {{monate}} months later. Until then it brings in no rent.
ex.loanLater: The fixed monthly payment for its loan only starts in {{start}}, with the last instalment to the developer. Before that you only pay interest on the loan drawn.
ex.loanSame: From handover, the fixed monthly payment for its loan runs as well.
ex.afterEnd: Your plan already ends before that, in {{ende}}.

m.exit: The joint sale at the end of your plan ({{jahr}}) is not in this timeline. What is left from it is shown in the section “{{s10}}”.
m.after: For at least one apartment you get the keys before it is fully paid. Rent already flows from handover, while the rest of the price goes to the developer in instalments. If the apartment is financed by the bank, the bank's fixed monthly payment only starts in the month of the last of these instalments.
m.refi: A refinancing is not a profit but an additional loan. In total you take on {{summe}} more this way. Your debt rises by this amount, and interest and repayment for it come on top of the other payments.
m.sameYear: If an apartment is bought and handed over in the same year, only the purchase appears in the timeline. You see the handover month on its card.
m.afterPlan: Entries after {{ende}} are after the end of your plan and no longer count in its numbers.
m.afterPlanSale: Entries after {{ende}} are after the end of your plan. Because it ends with the sale in {{ende}}, you no longer get rent from these handovers.

pitfalls.years: The timeline only shows years. Within a year, the entries are not sorted by month. The exact months are on the apartment cards.
pitfalls.equity: The equity at purchase flows with the instalments of the payment plan, not necessarily on the purchase date. It also includes the purchase costs.
pitfalls.refi: “werden wieder verfügbar” does not mean that money is left over. It is newly borrowed money.
pitfalls.dates: Handover dates are planned dates. If a handover moves, rent and monthly payment move with it.

properties.heading: How to read the apartment cards
properties.intro: There is one card per apartment. At the top you see the name, the purchase month and the handover month (handover means you get the keys, and letting starts). Below that you read from top to bottom: what the apartment costs and where the money comes from, how much rent it brings in the first year, what it is worth at the end and how much of it belongs to you. Everything is a model calculation with the assumptions on this page.

header.label: Purchase … · Handover …
header.text: Purchase is the month of the purchase contract, handover the month you get the keys. From handover the model counts rent.

model.label: Model property
model.text: Only in plans with reinvestment: an apartment the model buys later with reused money. A placeholder, not one that has already been chosen.

sold.label: SOLD {{y}}
sold.text: This apartment is sold on its own in the year shown. The card then has a coral border at the top. For the joint sale of all apartments at the end of your plan, this note does not appear.

price.label: Total price
price.text: Purchase price of the apartment including VAT, plus the furniture package if chosen. Purchase costs are not included.

equity.label: of which equity
equity.text: Your own money for this apartment. It also contains the purchase costs, in the model a flat 1 percent of the apartment price including VAT (without furniture). That is why the number is a little higher than your own share of the total price.

surplus.label: from rent and VAT refund
surplus.text: If there are instalments to the developer after handover, the surplus of your let apartments pays part of the purchase prices. Surplus means rent minus management, running costs, interest, repayments and taxes, plus the VAT refund. This line shows that part for this apartment. This money is neither starting capital nor a loan.

surplusRent.label: from rent
surplusRent.text: If there are instalments to the developer after handover, the surplus of your let apartments pays part of the purchase prices. Surplus means rent minus management, running costs, interest, repayments and taxes. This line shows that part for this apartment. This money is neither starting capital nor a loan.

loan.label: Loan
loan.text: How much the bank lends you for this apartment, counted at the start. It is the starting amount, not the debt at the end.

loanTable.label: Loan
loanTable.text: How much the bank lends you for this apartment, counted at the start. It is the starting amount, not the debt at the end. The same number is shown further down in the box “{{credLoans}}”.

creditSoFar.label: Loan drawn so far
creditSoFar.text: Shown instead of “Loan” if your plan ends, or the apartment is sold, before the bank's monthly payment starts. It is the loan you have drawn until then. You only pay interest on it. At a sale it is paid back from the proceeds.

openSale.label: open instalments, from the sale proceeds
openSale.text: Instalments to the developer that would only fall due after the sale. They are paid from the proceeds at the sale.

openAfter.label: open instalments after the period
openAfter.text: Instalments to the developer that only fall due after the end of your plan.

openCredit.label: Loan (equity not sufficient)
openCredit.text: Only for a cash purchase, meaning a purchase without a bank loan, when your equity does not fully cover the price. The gap runs as a loan on which you only pay interest.

rent.label: Rent in the first year
rent.text: The rental income in the calendar year of handover, counted only from the handover month. With a handover in December that is just one month. With a seasonal model (holiday letting with strong and weak months) each month counts with its seasonal share, and winter months bring little. It is income before management, running costs and taxes, so it is not your profit.

value.label: Value at the end
value.text: What the apartment is worth in the model at the end of your plan. It is calculated from the apartment price including VAT, without furniture, with the assumed growth per year, starting only at handover. If your plan ends with the joint sale, it is the value in the year of sale.

valueSale.label: Value at sale
valueSale.text: Shown instead of “Value at the end” if this apartment is sold on its own: its value in the year of sale, calculated the same way.

equityEnd.label: of which yours
equityEnd.text: Value minus the debts still on the apartment at that point: the remaining bank debt, instalments still open to the developer and loan drawn without a monthly payment. Selling costs and taxes at a sale are not yet deducted.

net.label: Proceeds after sale
net.text: Only for a single sale in a plan with reinvestment: what reaches you after the loan is paid off and selling costs, any repayment of the VAT refund and taxes are paid.

growth.label: Equity growth over {{n}} years
growth.text: A separate calculation for this apartment only, over {{n}} calendar years from the handover year. This is how it works: all surpluses of these years are added up. Years in which you have to put money in count as negative. Then the part of the apartment that belongs to you at the end of these years is added. The money put in is subtracted, and the result is divided by the money put in. The money put in counts as the total price plus purchase costs, minus “Loan” or “Loan drawn so far”. It is the growth over the whole period combined, not a return per year. If the line is missing, “of which equity” is less than 5 percent of the total price, and a percentage would not be meaningful.

loanTableModel.label: Loan
loanTableModel.text: How much the bank lends you for this apartment, counted at the start. It is the starting amount, not the debt at the end. For your own apartments, the same number is shown further down in the box “{{credLoans}}”. Model properties are not listed there.

equityEndEarly.label: of which yours
equityEndEarly.text: Value minus the debts still on the apartment at that point: the remaining bank debt, instalments still open to the developer and loan drawn without a monthly payment. Selling costs and taxes at a sale are not yet deducted. If your plan ends before an apartment's handover, this works differently on its card, see below.

ex.sum: On the first card, “of which equity” ({{ek}}){{weitere}} add up to {{summe}}. That is {{diff}} more than the total price of {{gesamt}}. The difference is the purchase costs contained in “of which equity”.
ex.sumOnly: On the first card, “of which equity” shows {{ek}}, which is {{diff}} more than the total price of {{gesamt}}. The difference is the purchase costs.
ex.onlyCosts: So no equity goes into the price itself here: “of which equity” is just the purchase costs.
ex.value: {{zeit}} the apartment is worth {{wert}} in the model. Of this, {{gehoert}} belongs to you. The remaining {{schuld}} is debt still on it at that point.
ex.valueFree: {{zeit}} the apartment is worth {{wert}} in the model. There is no debt left on it then, so “of which yours” is the full value.
ex.valueRefi: {{zeit}} the apartment is worth {{wert}} in the model. According to the card, {{gehoert}} of this belongs to you. The remaining {{schuld}} is debt from the purchase of this apartment that is still on it at that point. Loans from refinancing secured on this apartment are not deducted on the card.
ex.valueFreeRefi: {{zeit}} the apartment is worth {{wert}} in the model, and “of which yours” shows the full value. Loans from refinancing secured on this apartment are not deducted on the card.
ex.onlyCostsPooled: According to the card, no equity goes into the price itself: “of which equity” is just the purchase costs. In the instalment table further down in the section “{{credTitle}}”, however, your equity is spread over all apartments by date. That is why equity also appears there for this apartment.
ex.onlyCostsCard: According to the card, no equity goes into the price itself: “of which equity” is just the purchase costs.
ex.valueRefiLoan: {{zeit}} the apartment is worth {{wert}} in the model. According to the card, {{gehoert}} of this belongs to you. The remaining {{schuld}} is what is still owed on this apartment's loan. Loans from refinancing secured on this apartment are not deducted on the card.

m.rent1: On the first card, rent only starts in {{uebergabe}}. “Rent in the first year” ({{miete}}) therefore covers just one month.
m.rentN: On the first card, rent only starts in {{uebergabe}}. “Rent in the first year” ({{miete}}) therefore covers just {{n}} months.
m.rentFull: A full year of rent only comes from {{jahr}}.
m.surplus1: For one apartment, the surplus from {{quelle}} pays part of the purchase price, {{summe}}. Neither your starting capital nor the bank has to provide this part.
m.surplusN: For {{n}} apartments, the surplus from {{quelle}} pays part of the purchase price, {{summe}} in total. Neither your starting capital nor the bank has to provide this part.
m.openSale: Your plan ends with the sale before all instalments to the developer are paid. The {{summe}} still open is paid from the proceeds at the sale.
m.openSaleCredit: Your plan ends with the sale before all instalments to the developer are paid. The {{summe}} still open is paid from the proceeds at the sale, and so is the loan drawn until then.
m.openAfter: Your plan ends in {{ende}}, before all instalments to the developer are due. The remaining {{summe}} falls due after that.
m.openCredit1: For an apartment bought in cash, your equity is not quite enough. The missing {{summe}} runs as a loan on which you only pay interest. In the model it is not repaid: it is paid off at the sale or remains as debt at the end.
m.openCreditN: For {{n}} apartments bought in cash, your equity is not quite enough. The missing {{summe}} runs as a loan on which you only pay interest. In the model it is not repaid: it is paid off at the sale or remains as debt at the end.
m.sumEq: Together, {{karten}} show {{summe}} of equity. That is your starting capital of {{start}} plus {{nk}} of purchase costs.
m.exit: Your plan ends in {{jahr}} with the joint sale of all apartments. “Value at the end” and “of which yours” show the position in that year, before selling costs and taxes. What is really left after the sale is shown in the section “{{s10}}”.
m.growth: For the value, growth of {{g}} % per year is assumed, counted from handover. This is an assumption, not a promise.
m.growth0: No growth in value is assumed. “Value at the end” is therefore the apartment price including VAT, without furniture.
m.growthBaseEq: On the first card, the “Equity growth” of {{pct}} refers to “of which equity” ({{ek}}).
m.growthBase: On the first card, the “Equity growth” of {{pct}} does not refer only to “of which equity” but to {{basis}}: total price plus purchase costs, minus “{{kredit}}”.
m.growthBaseNoLoan: On the first card, the “Equity growth” of {{pct}} does not refer only to “of which equity” but to {{basis}}: total price plus purchase costs.
m.growthYears: It is calculated over {{n}} calendar years from the handover year, so {{von}} to {{bis}}.
m.growthBeyond: These years go beyond the end of your plan ({{ende}}). The growth is therefore a separate calculation for the apartment, not the result of your plan.
m.noGrowth1: For one apartment the line “Equity growth” is missing. This is intentional: there, “of which equity” is less than 5 percent of the total price, and a percentage on it would not be meaningful.
m.noGrowthN: For {{n}} apartments the line “Equity growth” is missing. This is intentional: there, “of which equity” is less than 5 percent of the total price, and a percentage on it would not be meaningful.
m.refi: Loans from refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) are not deducted on the card under “of which yours”. Your total debt is shown in the section “{{s6}}” under “{{fDebt}}”.
m.beforeHandover1: For one apartment your plan ends before handover. Its card still shows the value at the end of the handover year and the rent from handover.
m.beforeHandoverN: For {{n}} apartments your plan ends before handover. Their cards still show the value at the end of the handover year and the rent from handover.
m.beforeHandoverExit: What is really left at the sale is shown in the section “{{s10}}”.
m.overEquity: Together, {{karten}} show {{summe}} of equity, more than your starting capital of {{start}} provides. The reason: here the strategy always pays apartments without a bank loan (cash purchase) at their full price from equity. You would have to provide the difference on top.
m.sumEqExtra: Together, {{karten}} show {{summe}} of equity. That is your starting capital of {{start}} plus {{nk}} of purchase costs. So you pay the purchase costs on top of your starting capital.

pitfalls.costs: “of which equity” contains the purchase costs. If you add up the sources of money on a card, you therefore end up above the total price by that amount.
pitfalls.sumCards: If you add up “of which equity” on all cards, you get more than the equity that goes into the purchase prices. The difference is the purchase costs.
pitfalls.rent: “Rent in the first year” is usually not a full year and not a profit. With a handover late in the year the number is very small.
pitfalls.furniture: “Value at the end” is calculated without the furniture package. For an apartment with furniture, the value can therefore be below the total price at first.
pitfalls.growthStart: In the model, growth in value only starts at handover, not at purchase.
pitfalls.owned: “of which yours” is not the money you receive at a sale. Selling costs, taxes and, where applicable, a repayment of the VAT refund still have to be deducted.
pitfalls.roe: “Equity growth” is not a return per year. It always runs over the stated number of years from handover, even if your plan ends earlier. It calculates as if the bank loan ran from handover, and it deducts no selling costs. The return of your whole plan is shown in the section “{{s9}}” under “{{irr}}”.
pitfalls.round: Every number is rounded to whole euros. If you recalculate, it can be off by 1 €.
pitfalls.sumCardsOwn: If you add up “of which equity” on the cards of your own apartments (without model properties), you get more than the equity that goes into their purchase prices. The difference is the purchase costs.

karten.own: the cards of your own apartments (without model properties)

bh.none2: “of which yours” deducts neither the instalments still open nor {{kredit}}
bh.rates: “of which yours” does not deduct the instalments still open

exit.heading: How to read the sale calculation
exit.intro: This table plays through what happens when the apartments are sold. Each row is one apartment: on the left the assumed sale price (Value column), then everything that is deducted from it, and on the far right what is left (Proceeds column). {{mode}} Everything is a model calculation with assumed prices, not a promise.

obj.label: Apartment
obj.text: The apartment this row is about.

year.label: Sale
year.text: The year in which the sale is assumed. The model sells at the end of the year, so that year's rent is still fully included in the cash flow table. The year of the first purchase counts as the first year: your first purchase is in {{first}}, the sale comes after {{n}} years, so at the end of {{year}}.

yearOne.label: Sale
yearOne.text: The year in which the sale is assumed. The model sells at the end of the year, so that year's rent is still fully included in the cash flow table. The year of the first purchase counts as the first year: your first purchase is in {{first}}, the sale comes after one year, so already at the end of {{year}}.

yearGeneric.label: Sale
yearGeneric.text: The year in which the sale is assumed. The model sells at the end of the year, so that year's rent is still fully included in the cash flow table. The year of the first purchase counts as the first year.

yearSingle.label: Sale
yearSingle.text: The year in which the model sells this apartment. The sale happens at the end of the year, so that year's rent is still fully included in the cash flow table.

value.label: Value
value.text: The assumed sale price at the end of the year. It is based on the purchase price including VAT (value added tax). From the handover of the finished apartment it grows every year by the assumed increase in value, not before. Furniture is not included. If an apartment has not been handed over at the time of sale, this column only shows what has been paid to the developer so far, without any increase in value. The developer is the company that builds the apartment and sells it to you.

debt.label: Loan
debt.text: All debts that have to be paid off at the sale: the remaining bank loan, instalments still owed to the developer after handover, and any bridging loan still open. A bridging loan is borrowed money for instalments that fall due while the actual bank loan has not been paid out yet.{{ri}}{{cash}} The minus shows that this amount is deducted from the value.

costs.label: Costs
costs.text: The costs of the sale: estate agent and lawyer, each plus 19% Cypriot VAT on their invoice, plus the transfer levy. This is a charge of 0.4% of the sale price that is due in Cyprus every time a property changes hands. In the model the seller pays it, which is you. Agent and lawyer are calculated from the value in the same row.{{joint}}

vat.label: VAT
vat.text: This column only appears if at least one row has an amount here. That only happens with short-term letting, meaning letting to holiday guests. In that case the state refunds you the VAT on the purchase price (VAT refund). You may only keep it for good once the apartment has been let this way for ten years. If you sell earlier, you pay back the share for the missing years: that is an amount with a minus. Each year from handover reduces the repayment by one tenth, and both the handover year and the sale year count in full. An amount with a plus (green) means the refund had not reached you yet at the time of sale. You still receive it, but only the share for the years up to the sale. An empty cell means nothing to pay back and nothing more to receive.

tax.label: Taxes
tax.text: The taxes on the sale. They include the Cypriot capital gains tax, the tax on the profit from the sale: 20% of that profit. The profit is the value minus the purchase price (with VAT) and the purchase costs, both increased by the assumed inflation, meaning general price increases, for every year between purchase and sale (in your plan {{cpi}}% a year), minus agent and lawyer. Purchase costs are the incidental costs of buying, 1% of the purchase price in the model. For an apartment not yet handed over, the model calculates no profit.{{extra}}

net.label: Proceeds
net.text: What is left after all deductions: {{formula}}{{joint}} The proceeds are not your profit, because they also contain the money you put in yourself.

total.label: Total
total.text: The sum of all apartments. {{cols}} are exactly the rows above added up. Taxes and proceeds only exist in this row.{{checks}}

eb.label: Plus: equity reserved for the remaining instalments that is no longer needed
eb.text: Only appears if instalments to the developer would still have been due after the sale. You had held back equity, meaning your own money, for these instalments. Because of the sale you no longer have to pay them from that money: after handover, open instalments are paid from the sale price (they are then included in the Loan column), before handover they lapse with the sale. The money you held back belongs to you and comes on top of the proceeds. It is not yet included in the Proceeds figure.

pitfalls.profit: Proceeds are not profit. The proceeds also contain the money you put in yourself at the start. You only see what you have earned once you deduct the money you put in and add the surpluses of the years before the sale (cash flow table).
pitfalls.empty: Empty cells for taxes and proceeds in the apartment rows do not mean 0 €. In a joint sale the tax is calculated for all apartments together and only appears in the Total row.
pitfalls.debt: "Loan" is not only the bank. Instalments still owed to the developer and an open bridging loan are also paid off at the sale and appear in this column.
pitfalls.vat: A minus in the VAT column means you pay back. A plus (green) means you still receive money. This is not a second refund but the part of the first one not yet paid out, reduced to the years up to the sale.
pitfalls.eb: The row "Plus: equity reserved ..." is not included in the proceeds. Add it if you want to know what you have in total after the sale. "Proceeds after sale" at the top does not include it either.
pitfalls.firstYear: The year of the first purchase counts as the first year, even if you only buy in the autumn. So the time between purchase and sale is often almost a year shorter than the number of years suggests.
pitfalls.broker: Agent and lawyer cost more than their percentages in the plan, because in Cyprus 19% VAT is added to their invoice. This is already included in "Costs".
pitfalls.value: The value is an assumption based on the yearly increase in value, not an offer and not a valuation. A lower sale price reduces the proceeds directly.

ex.main: This is how you check {{row}}: {{value}} value minus {{debt}} loan minus {{costs}} costs{{vat}} minus {{tax}} taxes = {{net}}. {{end}}{{eb}}
ex.vatPlus: plus {{v}} VAT refund still to come
ex.endPos: These are the proceeds: the money left over after the sale in {{year}}.
ex.endNeg: The proceeds are negative: the sale price is not enough to cover {{list}}. You would have to pay the difference out of your own pocket in {{year}}.
ex.eb: On top of that come {{eb}} of equity that was set aside for instalments and is no longer needed. Altogether you have {{sum}} after the sale.
ex.ebOnly: On top of that come {{eb}} of equity that was set aside for instalments and is no longer needed.
ex.endNegRi: The proceeds are negative: the sale price is not enough to cover {{list}}. In the model the difference comes off the account balance in {{year}}.
ex.endNegShort: The proceeds are negative: the sale price is not enough to cover {{list}}.
ex.ebCovers: On top of that come {{eb}} of equity that was set aside for instalments and is no longer needed. It covers the difference, and you are left with {{sum}} after the sale.
ex.ebShort: On top of that come {{eb}} of equity that was set aside for instalments and is no longer needed. Even so, {{s}} is still missing, which you would have to pay out of your own pocket in {{year}}.

m.introJoint: In your plan all apartments are sold together at the end. The tax is then calculated for all apartments together, which is why taxes and proceeds only appear in the Total row.
m.introSingle: In your plan apartments are sold one by one, each in its own year of sale. Every apartment that is sold has its own row with its own taxes and its own proceeds.{{kept}}
m.debtRi: It also includes the share of loans from refinancing. Refinancing means a new loan on an apartment you already own.
m.costsJoint: In a joint sale the transfer levy is calculated for all apartments together and split across the rows by value.
m.taxAllowPriv: As a private person you have a once-in-a-lifetime allowance, meaning a tax-free amount: 30.000 € per person, 60.000 € for a couple.
m.taxAllowFirm: A company has no allowance, meaning no tax-free amount.
m.taxDe: Because you are tax resident in Germany and buy privately, the German tax on the sale profit is added if less than ten years lie between purchase and sale. The Cypriot tax is credited against it, meaning deducted from it.
m.taxDivJoint: Because you buy through a company, the Total row also contains the tax on the dividend, meaning on paying out the proceeds from the company to you.
m.taxWhereJoint: The tax only appears in the Total row.
m.taxWhereSingle: Every row has its own tax.
m.netFormulaVat: value minus loan minus costs minus VAT minus taxes. If the VAT column shows a plus, that amount is added.
m.netFormula: value minus loan minus costs minus taxes.
m.netJoint: In a joint sale the proceeds only appear in the Total row.
m.totalNet: The proceeds here are exactly the figure "Proceeds after sale" at the top of the page.
m.totalDebtSame: The loan is the same as "Loan at the end" at the top.
m.totalDebtRound: The loan differs from "Loan at the end" at the top by {{d}} because of rounding. This is not an error in the calculation.
m.totalValueSame: The value is the same as "Value of the properties" at the top.
m.totalValueDiff: The value is not the same as "Value of the properties" at the top, because at least one apartment has not been handed over at the time of sale.
m.growth: The value is based on the assumption that the apartments gain {{g}}% in value every year from handover. If prices rise more slowly, the proceeds fall directly.
m.growth0: This plan assumes no increase in value: the apartments are sold at the price they were bought for. After selling costs and purchase costs, less is left than the apartments cost.
m.cent: Of every euro of sale price, about {{cent}} cents remain as proceeds in this model. The rest goes to {{list}}.
m.costPct: Your plan assumes: agent {{broker}}%, lawyer {{lawyer}}%, both plus 19% VAT, plus 0.4% transfer levy. Together that is about {{pct}}% of the sale price.
m.vatBack: You are selling before the end of the ten years that the VAT refund is tied to. That is why {{v}} of the refunded VAT goes back to the state. The later you sell, the smaller this amount.
m.vatOpen1: For one apartment the VAT refund had not reached you yet at the time of sale. You still receive it, but only the share for the years up to the sale: {{v}}. This amount appears with a plus in the VAT column and increases your proceeds.
m.vatOpenN: For {{n}} apartments the VAT refund had not reached you yet at the time of sale. You still receive it, but only the share for the years up to the sale: {{v}} in total. These amounts appear with a plus in the VAT column and increase your proceeds.
m.openRest: At the time of sale, instalments to the developer are still running. The open {{v}} are included in the Loan column and are paid from the sale price.
m.notReady1: One apartment has not been handed over at the time of sale. For it, the value is only what has been paid to the developer so far, without any increase in value. Agent, lawyer and transfer levy still apply, and the purchase costs have been spent. So less comes back for this apartment than went into it.
m.notReadyN: {{n}} apartments have not been handed over at the time of sale. For them, the value is only what has been paid to the developer so far, without any increase in value. Agent, lawyer and transfer levy still apply, and the purchase costs have been spent. So less comes back for these apartments than went into them.
m.deTax: You are tax resident in Germany and buy privately. If less than ten years lie between purchase and sale, the sale profit is also taxable in Germany, at your tax rate from the plan ({{rate}}%). The depreciation increases the profit. Depreciation is the yearly loss in value of the building that you deducted from your taxes in the years before. The Cypriot tax is credited, so you do not pay twice.{{always}}
m.deTaxAlways: In your plan the sale falls within these ten years.
m.firmJoint: You buy through a company. The proceeds first belong to the company. If it pays them out to you (dividend), tax is due: in the plan {{payout}}% are paid out and taxed at {{rate}}%. Here this tax is {{div}} and it is already included in the Taxes column. The model calculates it on the whole proceeds before the payout, not only on the profit.{{rest}}
m.firmJointRest: What is not paid out stays in the company but is counted in the proceeds.
m.firmSingle: You buy through a company and sell apartments one by one. For these sales the model calculates no tax on a payout to you. If you later have the company pay out the proceeds to you, this tax comes on top.
m.introKept: Apartments you keep until the end do not appear here.
m.debtCash: In your plan your starting capital is not enough for the equity of all purchases. The loan that covers this gap is also included in this column.

costKpis.heading: How to read the four tiles
costKpis.intro: The four tiles sum up how much of your own money is in the purchases, whether you have to add money along the way, what the financing costs in interest and how much wealth has been added at the end. All figures apply to the period of this evaluation, {{period}}.{{sale}}

equity.label: Equity invested
equity.text: Your own money for the purchase prices and purchase costs of the apartments you start with{{ri}}. Equity is the part you pay yourself rather than the bank. Purchase costs are the incidental costs of buying, 1% of the purchase price in the model. The tile shows at most your starting capital. You can see the full amount including purchase costs in the table below under "In Immobilien gebunden" (tied up in property).

add0.label: Additional capital needed
add0.text: "no" means: if you add up the cash flow of all years so far, the total is not negative at the end of any year. Cash flow is the money left over or missing in a year after all running payments. Individual years can still be negative if surpluses from earlier years cover the gap.

add0Ri.label: Additional capital needed
add0Ri.text: "no" means: the account balance in the model does not fall below zero at the end of any year.

add0Old.label: Additional capital needed
add0Old.text: In your plan the page does not check this, so it always says "no". Whether and when you have to add money in individual years is shown by a negative cash flow in the cash flow table. Cash flow is the money left over or missing in a year after all running payments.

add.label: Additional capital needed
add.text: Appears instead of "no" when the cash flow of all years so far, added up, is negative at the end of a year. Cash flow is the money left over or missing in a year after all running payments. The amount is the lowest point of this total, so it is how much you would have to add out of your own pocket at that point.{{nk}}

addRi.label: Additional capital needed
addRi.text: Appears instead of "no" when the account balance in the model falls below zero at the end of a year. The amount is the lowest point, so it is how much you would have to add at that point.

interest.label: Interest over the period
interest.text: All interest in the period of this evaluation. Interest is the price you pay for someone lending you money. It includes interest on the bank loan, on instalments still owed to the developer (the company that builds and sells) after handover, and on a bridging loan, meaning borrowed money for instalments due while the bank loan has not been paid out yet{{ri}}. This money is gone. Repayment, meaning paying back the loan itself, is not included. The figure covers only the period on this page, not the full term of the loan.

gain.label: Increase in wealth
gain.text: Your net worth at the end minus your starting capital. Net worth is what belongs to you after all debts are deducted: value of the apartments minus loans, plus instalments already paid for apartments not yet handed over, plus liquidity, meaning money you can use right away. It is the position before any sale: selling costs, VAT repayment and tax on the sale are not yet deducted, and the surpluses of the individual years are not included.{{nk}}

gainBound.label: Increase in wealth
gainBound.text: Your net worth at the end minus the money that went into the purchases: {{v}}, the figure under "In Immobilien gebunden" (tied up in property) in the table below, including purchase costs. Your starting capital is larger. The unused rest does not appear anywhere on this page and is therefore not deducted either. Net worth is what belongs to you after all debts are deducted: value of the apartments minus loans, plus instalments already paid for apartments not yet handed over, plus liquidity, meaning money you can use right away. It is the position before any sale: selling costs, VAT repayment and tax on the sale are not yet deducted, and the surpluses of the individual years are not included.

gainBoundHeld.label: Increase in wealth
gainBoundHeld.text: Your net worth at the end minus the money that went into the purchases: {{v}}, the figure under "In Immobilien gebunden" (tied up in property) in the table below, including purchase costs. Not deducted is the money from your starting capital that was set aside for later instalments and appears under "Liquidität am Ende" (liquidity at the end), even though it counts towards net worth. Net worth is what belongs to you after all debts are deducted: value of the apartments minus loans, plus instalments already paid for apartments not yet handed over, plus liquidity, meaning money you can use right away. It is the position before any sale: selling costs, VAT repayment and tax on the sale are not yet deducted, and the surpluses of the individual years are not included.

gainBoundLiq.label: Increase in wealth
gainBoundLiq.text: Your net worth at the end minus the money from your starting capital that the plan needs: {{v}}, that is "In Immobilien gebunden" (tied up in property) plus "Liquidität am Ende" (liquidity at the end) from the table below. Your starting capital is larger. The unused rest does not appear anywhere on this page and is therefore not deducted either. Net worth is what belongs to you after all debts are deducted: value of the apartments minus loans, plus instalments already paid for apartments not yet handed over, plus liquidity, meaning money you can use right away. It is the position before any sale: selling costs, VAT repayment and tax on the sale are not yet deducted, and the surpluses of the individual years are not included.

gainRi.label: Increase in wealth
gainRi.text: Your net worth at the end minus your starting capital. Net worth is what belongs to you after all debts are deducted: value of the apartments minus loans, plus instalments already paid for apartments not yet handed over, plus liquidity, meaning money you can use right away. Liquidity here is the account balance of the model at the end. For the apartments you still own at the end, selling costs and taxes are not deducted.

gainOther.label: Increase in wealth
gainOther.text: Your net worth at the end minus the capital you put in. Net worth is what belongs to you after all debts are deducted: value of the apartments minus loans, plus instalments already paid for apartments not yet handed over, plus liquidity, meaning money you can use right away.

addNet.label: Additional capital needed
addNet.text: Appears instead of "no" when the cash flow of all years so far, added up, is negative at the end of a year and your unused starting capital does not fully cover the gap. Cash flow is the money left over or missing in a year after all running payments. The amount is the lowest point of this total minus your unused starting capital, so it is how much extra you would have to add out of your own pocket at that point.{{nk}}

add0Unused.label: Additional capital needed
add0Unused.text: "no" means: if you add up the cash flow of all years so far, the total does turn negative at the end of a year, but your unused starting capital covers this gap. Cash flow is the money left over or missing in a year after all running payments.

gainBoundDouble.label: Increase in wealth
gainBoundDouble.text: Your net worth at the end minus the amount under "In Immobilien gebunden" (tied up in property) in the table below: {{v}}, including purchase costs. It also counts equity for instalments that would only fall due {{when}} and will no longer be paid. The same money counts towards net worth as liquidity, so the two cancel out. Your starting capital is larger. The unused rest does not appear anywhere on this page and is therefore not deducted either. Net worth is what belongs to you after all debts are deducted: value of the apartments minus loans, plus instalments already paid for apartments not yet handed over, plus liquidity, meaning money you can use right away. It is the position before any sale: selling costs, VAT repayment and tax on the sale are not yet deducted, and the surpluses of the individual years are not included.

pitfalls.capital: "Capital invested" at the very top is your starting capital. "Equity invested" here is the part that goes into purchase prices and purchase costs, but at most your starting capital. The two figures can differ.
pitfalls.no: "no" does not mean that money is left over every year. You can spot years in which you have to add money by a negative cash flow in the cash flow table.
pitfalls.amount: The amount under "Additional capital needed" is not the sum of all top-ups but only the lowest point. What you add in the individual years is shown in the cash flow table.
pitfalls.gain: The increase in wealth is not an account balance and not sale proceeds. It uses the value of the apartments before a sale. After selling costs and taxes, less is left.
pitfalls.gainRi: The increase in wealth is not an account balance. It uses the value of the apartments you own at the end, without selling costs and taxes.
pitfalls.interest: "Interest over the period" only covers the period on this page. Without a sale, the loan and interest continue afterwards.
pitfalls.amort: Repayment is not an expense like interest. It reduces your loan and increases your equity, which is why it is not in the interest tile.

moneyFlow.heading: How to read the capital flow table
moneyFlow.intro: The table shows the big money flows of the strategy, each as a total over the whole period of the evaluation. Each row is one kind of money: what flows in, what flows out and what only changes place. Green amounts flow to you or belong to you, orange amounts with a minus flow out. The column "What that means" says in one sentence whether the money is gone or, for example, sits in the apartments as equity. The row names and that column are currently shown in German. Important: the table is not an account statement. Added together, the rows do not give the last row.

amount.label: Amount
amount.text: The total over all years of the period. Orange with a minus: money flows out. Green without a minus: money flows in or is available.

meaning.label: What that means
meaning.text: A short explanation of whether the money is gone or only changes place.

start.label: Startkapital
start.text: Starting capital: the money you start with according to the plan. It is the same figure as "Capital invested" at the very top.

bound.label: In Immobilien gebunden
bound.text: Tied up in property: your own money for the purchase prices of the apartments you start with, plus the purchase costs, meaning the incidental costs of buying (1% of the purchase price including VAT in the model). The part for the purchase prices is not gone, it sits in the apartments as equity. The purchase costs, on the other hand, are spent and are not part of the apartments' value.{{mode}}

rent.label: Mieteinnahmen
rent.text: Rental income: all rents the apartments bring in during the period, before running costs, interest and taxes. There is no rent before the handover of the finished apartment.

costs.label: Laufende Kosten
costs.text: Running costs: management, community fees including insurance and the maintenance reserve, meaning money for later repairs. This money is gone.

interest.label: Zinsen
interest.text: Interest: all interest in the period, the same figure as in the tile "Interest over the period". This money is gone.

amort.label: Tilgung
amort.text: Repayment: what you pay back on the bank loan{{ri}}. The money leaves your account, but your debt with the bank falls by exactly this amount. Instalments to the developer, the company that builds and sells, are part of the purchase price and do not appear here.

taxes.label: Steuern und Abgaben
taxes.text: Taxes and contributions: the running taxes in the period, the same figure as "Total taxes and contributions" in the Taxes section. It includes income tax, health contribution, social insurance and also the tax in Germany, and for a company the company's profit tax and the tax on dividends.{{sale}} A green amount without a minus means that on balance you save tax.

vat.label: MwSt-Erstattung
vat.text: VAT refund: only with short-term letting, the VAT on the purchase price that the state pays back to you, once per apartment. In the model it arrives about 18 months after handover. Only refunds that arrive within the period are shown here.{{sale}}

refi.label: Refinanzierung
refi.text: Refinancing: money from a new loan on apartments you already own. It flows to you, but increases your debt by the same amount. It is not a profit.

sale.label: Verkaufserlöse
sale.text: Sale proceeds: what is left from the sale after loan, costs, VAT repayment and taxes. This is the proceeds figure from the Total row of the sale table. If the amount is orange with a minus, the sale price is not enough for loan, costs and taxes.

saleRi.label: Verkaufserlöse
saleRi.text: Sale proceeds: what is left from the sales after loan, costs, VAT repayment and taxes, the sum of the proceeds of all individual sales in the sale table. If the amount is orange with a minus, the sale price is not enough for loan, costs and taxes.

liq.label: Liquidität am Ende
liq.text: Liquidity at the end: liquidity means money you can use right away. In your plan, however, this row only counts money set aside for instalments to the developer that would only fall due {{when}}. The surpluses of the individual years{{sale}} are not included.

liqRi.label: Liquidität am Ende
liqRi.text: Liquidity at the end: liquidity means money you can use right away. Here it is the account balance of the model at the end.

boundGap.label: In Immobilien gebunden
boundGap.text: Tied up in property: the equity that the purchases of the apartments you start with need, plus the purchase costs, meaning the incidental costs of buying (1% of the purchase price including VAT in the model). In your plan this is more than your starting capital. In the model a loan covers the missing part, so this row also contains borrowed money. The purchase costs are spent and are not part of the apartments' value.{{mode}}

pitfalls.notAccount: Added together, the rows do not give "Liquidität am Ende" (liquidity at the end). The table is not an account statement: what the bank pays towards the purchase price, the instalments to the developer and further purchases do not appear as separate rows.
pitfalls.liq: In your plan, "Liquidität am Ende" (liquidity at the end) is not your account balance at the end. The row only counts money set aside for instalments. Sale proceeds and surpluses appear in separate rows or in the cash flow table.
pitfalls.bound: "In Immobilien gebunden" (tied up in property) is mostly not a loss, the money sits in the apartments as equity. Only the purchase costs included in it are really spent.
pitfalls.unpaid: In your plan "In Immobilien gebunden" and "Liquidität am Ende" both contain the same {{liq}} of equity that was never paid. So do not add the two rows together.

pitfalls.taxDe: "Steuern und Abgaben" (taxes and contributions) also contains the tax in Germany, even though the explanation next to it does not mention it.
pitfalls.vat: You may only keep the VAT refund in full if the apartment is let this way for ten years. If you sell earlier, part of it goes back (sale table, VAT column).
pitfalls.tile: "Equity invested" in the tile above and "In Immobilien gebunden" can differ. The tile shows at most your starting capital, the table the full amount including purchase costs.

m.taxGreen: "Steuern und Abgaben" shows a green amount: on balance you save {{v}} in taxes over the period. In the model, the tax losses from the apartments reduce your tax in Germany.

taxes.heading: How to read the tax tiles
taxes.intro: The tiles show which taxes and contributions arise in the model, each added up over the whole period of the evaluation, {{period}}.{{sale}} A tile that is missing is 0 € in your plan. An amount with a minus is a tax saving, not a debt.

income.label: Income tax
income.text: The tax in Cyprus on the profit from letting, added up over the whole period. Profit here means rent minus deductible costs, interest and depreciation. Depreciation is the yearly loss in value of building and furniture that you may deduct from your taxes. For long-term letting, Cyprus deducts a flat 20% of the rent instead of the actual costs. The first 22.000 € of income per person and year are tax-free in Cyprus, so twice for a couple.{{cy}} Not included are the tax in Germany, health contribution, social insurance and the tax on the sale.

incomeFirm.label: Income tax
incomeFirm.text: Because you buy through a company, this shows the Cypriot corporation tax, meaning the company's profit tax, added up over the whole period. Profit here means rent minus costs, interest and depreciation. Depreciation is the yearly loss in value of building and furniture that the company may deduct from its taxes. A company has no tax-free amount like private persons. Not included are the tax on dividends paid to you and the tax on the sale.

total.label: Total taxes and contributions
total.text: All running taxes and contributions in the period together: income tax plus health contribution plus social insurance plus tax in Germany. The tax on the sale is not included. The same figure appears in the capital flow table under "Steuern und Abgaben" (taxes and contributions).

year.label: Average per year
year.text: "Total taxes and contributions" divided by the number of years in the period. Years without rent, such as the construction period, are counted too. In individual years the tax can be much higher or lower than this average.

exit.label: Tax on the sale
exit.text: {{what}}: the Cypriot capital gains tax, 20% of the sale profit{{allow}}{{de}}. It is not included in "Total taxes and contributions".{{firm}}

gesy.label: Health contribution
gesy.text: The Cypriot health contribution (GESY), only if you buy privately and live in Cyprus. It is 2.65% of the rental income, up to a ceiling. If your short-term letting counts as self-employment, it is 4% of the profit instead. It is not an income tax and is also due when no income tax arises.

si.label: Social insurance
si.text: Only if you buy privately, live in Cyprus and the short-term letting counts as self-employment: 16.6% of the profit, calculated on at least a fixed minimum income of 20.318 € a year and at most on 68.904 €. It is due from the first year with rent, even if the profit is smaller.

de.label: Tax in Germany
de.text: You buy privately and are tax resident in Germany. This shows the German income tax on the rental profit, at your tax rate from the plan ({{rate}}%). The income tax paid in Cyprus is deducted from it (credit), so you do not pay twice. In years with a tax loss the value is negative, which is a saving. The tax on the sale is not included here.

deFirm.label: Tax in Germany
deFirm.text: Because you buy through a company, this shows the tax on the profits the company pays out to you as dividends.{{cy}} The tax on the sale is not included here.

pitfalls.notAll: "Total taxes and contributions" does not mean "all taxes". The tax on the sale has its own tile and is not included there.
pitfalls.zero: "Income tax 0 €" does not mean tax-free. It only refers to the Cypriot income tax.{{tiles}}
pitfalls.zeroFirm: "Income tax 0 €" does not mean tax-free. It only refers to the company's corporation tax.{{de}} A company pays no health contribution on the rents.
pitfalls.gesy: You only pay the health contribution if you buy privately and live in Cyprus. If its tile is missing, it does not apply to you.
pitfalls.minus: A minus is a saving. In the model it assumes that you have other income in Germany whose tax is reduced by it.
pitfalls.avg: "Average per year" also spreads the tax over years without rent. The figures for each year are in the cash flow table in the "Taxes" column.
pitfalls.firm: For a company, "Tax in Germany" is the tax on dividends, even if you live in Cyprus.{{sale}}
pitfalls.model: All tax figures are a simplified model calculation with the rates from the plan, not tax advice.
pitfalls.firmNoDe: With a company, the profits it pays out to you as dividends are taxed separately. The tile for this ("Tax in Germany") is missing because the model charges no such tax on the running income.{{sale}}
