scenarios.heading: How to read the three developments
scenarios.intro: The table runs your strategy through three times in full. Each column is a possible development of the market, each row a metric. The values apply to the end of the last year ({{lastYear}}){{saleYearNote}}. Only “{{scCf}}” adds up all years. Your own apartments, their purchase prices and the period are the same in all three columns.{{introRi}}{{sameNote}}

metric.label: Metric
metric.text: What the row measures. Every metric is explained here.

basis.label: As planned
basis.text: Your strategy with its own assumptions: {{gB}} % appreciation per year, {{rgB}} % rent growth per year, {{iB}} % interest on bank loans and a maintenance reserve of {{mB}} % of the purchase price per year.{{clampNote}}

cons.label: Cautious
cons.text: A weaker world in which several things go worse at the same time. The apartments gain less value: {{gK}} % instead of {{gB}} % per year (2 percentage points less, never below 0 %). Rents rise more slowly: {{rgK}} % instead of {{rgB}} % per year (1 percentage point less, never below 0 %). Interest on all bank loans is {{iK}} % instead of {{iB}} % (1 percentage point more), from the very first day. The maintenance reserve rises to {{mK}} % instead of {{mB}} % of the purchase price per year. A fixed monthly rent that was entered is also cut by 10 %, for example for vacancy. For apartments whose rent is calculated from occupancy and price per night (season model), this cut does not apply. The interest a developer charges on instalments after handover stays the same.{{consRi}}

opt.label: Favourable
opt.text: A better world: {{gO}} % instead of {{gB}} % appreciation per year (2 percentage points more), {{rgO}} % instead of {{rgB}} % rent growth per year (1 percentage point more), {{iO}} % instead of {{iB}} % interest on bank loans (0,5 percentage points less, never below 0,1 %) and {{mO}} % instead of {{mB}} % maintenance reserve (never below 0 %). A fixed monthly rent that was entered rises by 5 %, again not with the season model.{{optRi}}

units.label: Apartments
units.text: How many apartments belong to your strategy. All purchased apartments are counted, including one that is still being built at the end.{{unitsSold}} Because no further purchases are added in your strategy, the number is the same in all three columns.

unitsRI.label: Apartments
unitsRI.text: How many apartments you own at the end that have been handed over and not sold. The apartments the model buys in addition are included. Depending on the development it can finance more or fewer of them, which is why the columns can differ.

value.label: Property value at the end
value.text: What your handed-over apartments are worth together at the end of the year, projected with the appreciation of each column. Apartments still under construction do not count here yet.{{valueSold}}{{valueNote}}

debt.label: Loan outstanding
debt.text: All debts still open at the end of the year: the rest of the bank loans, instalments still owed to the developer after handover and, if needed, a bridging loan. A bridging loan is a short loan that covers instalments until the bank pays out the actual loan.{{debtRi}}{{debtNote}}

worth.label: Net worth
worth.text: Property value minus the loan outstanding. Added to this, if there are any, are purchase instalments you have already paid for an apartment that has not been handed over yet, and money set aside for instalments to the developer. The cash flow of the individual years is not included, it is shown in “{{scCf}}”.{{worthNote}}

worthRI.label: Net worth
worthRI.text: What belongs to you at the end once all debts are deducted: property value minus the loan outstanding plus the money in your account (liquidity). Costs and taxes of a later sale are not deducted.

irr.label: Return per year
irr.text: The average interest your invested money earns per year (technical term: internal rate of return). Imagine a savings account: at what fixed interest rate per year would your money have had to grow there to reach the same result? It matters when money flows. Money that comes back early counts for more than money that comes back late. {{how}}{{dash}}

cf.label: Cash flow combined
cf.text: All yearly cash flows of the period added up. Cash flow means: rents minus costs, interest (the price of the loan), repayment (the part of the instalment that reduces the debt) and taxes{{vatPlus}}.{{vat}}{{payNote}}{{sumSentence}} Positive means: money was left over in the end. {{negNote}} {{where}}

rec.label: Capital recycling
rec.text: The capital recycling factor of that column: your own money that flows again as equity into further apartments in the model, divided by your starting capital. It is not a profit and not a return. More on this in the section “{{s4}}”.

exit.label: Proceeds after sale
exit.text: What actually reaches you from the planned sale at the end: sale price minus repayment of all loans, minus selling costs (agent and lawyer, plus a small transfer fee) and minus taxes on the gain{{firma}}.{{vatRepay}}{{vatOpenNote}}

exitNone.label: Proceeds after sale
exitNone.text: What would reach you from a planned sale at the end, after repaying the loans, after selling costs and taxes. No sale is planned in your strategy, which is why a dash is shown here.

ex.p_sale: , which is the year of the planned sale
ex.p_ri: How many further apartments the model buys, however, can change from column to column.
ex.p_same: Numbers that appear both in the column “{{scBasis}}” in bold and in “{{s1}}” at the top are the same.
ex.p_sameButUnits: Property value, loan, net worth and return in the column “{{scBasis}}” in bold are the same as in “{{s1}}” at the top. Only the row “{{scUnits}}” counts differently, see below.
ex.p_consRi: The purchase prices of further apartments the model buys also rise 2 percentage points more slowly (never below 0 %). For these further apartments the 10 % rent cut always applies.
ex.p_optRi: The purchase prices of further apartments rise 2 percentage points faster accordingly. For these further apartments the 5 % rent increase always applies.
ex.p_valueSale: For you this is the value in the year of the planned sale, i.e. the assumed sale price before costs and taxes.
ex.p_debtRi: Added to this are additional loans the bank later grants on apartments already handed over (refinancing).
ex.p_debtSale: For you this is the balance just before the sale. It is repaid from the sale price.
ex.p_worthSale: For you this is the position before selling costs and taxes.
ex.p_irrSale: It counts your equity in the year you pay it in, the cash flow of every year and, at the end, the proceeds after sale, i.e. after costs and taxes.
ex.p_irrHold: It counts your equity in the year you pay it in, the cash flow of every year and, at the end, property value minus loan (plus purchase instalments already paid for apartments under construction). Costs and taxes of a sale are not deducted.
ex.p_irrRi: It counts only your starting capital in the first year{{contrib}} and your net worth at the end. The surpluses of the years stay in the strategy and are already part of the end value. Costs and taxes of a later sale are not deducted.
ex.p_irrDash: If a dash is shown here, no return can be calculated for this period.
ex.p_cfVat: VAT refund means: with short-term letting you get the VAT on the purchase price back once.
ex.p_cfPay: The part that goes into instalments to the developer (column “{{tToPay}}”) is already deducted.
ex.p_cfOut: This money has already reached you over the years, or come from you. It is not part of the net worth.
ex.p_cfRi: With reinvestment nothing is paid out: the cash flow stays in the strategy, in the account or as equity in further apartments. So it is already part of the net worth.
ex.p_firma: , minus the tax on the dividend from your company to you
ex.pBoth: purchase instalments already paid and money set aside
ex.pPaid: purchase instalments already paid for apartments under construction
ex.pHeld: money set aside in your account
ex.pBothD: purchase instalments already paid and money set aside
ex.pPaidD: purchase instalments already paid for apartments under construction
ex.pHeldD: money set aside in your account
ex.aValue: In {{y}} your apartments are worth {{wert}} together. The loan still outstanding, {{kredit}}, is deducted from this.
ex.aRestPlus: Add {{plus}} for {{what}}. That gives {{netto}} net worth ({{eqnPlus}}).
ex.aNoValue: In {{y}} none of your apartments has been handed over yet, which is why the property value shows {{wert}}.
ex.aOnlyPaid: Your net worth of {{netto}} consists of {{whatD}}.
ex.aBack: In addition you keep {{back}} of equity that was set aside for later instalments and is no longer needed because of the sale.
ex.wVat: a partial repayment of the VAT refund
ex.aDeduct: On the sale, {{whatDeduct}} are still deducted, {{abzug}} in total. What remains is {{erloes}} ({{eqnExit}}), which is the row “{{scExit}}”.
ex.aLeftPlain: After repaying the loans, after selling costs and taxes, {{erloes}} remain from the sale (row “{{scExit}}”).
ex.cfPos: On top of that come {{cf}} of cash flow that have already reached you over the years (row “{{scCf}}”).
ex.cfPosHold: In addition, {{cf}} of cash flow have reached you over the years (row “{{scCf}}”).
ex.cfNeg: Over the years you have also paid in {{cf}} (row “{{scCf}}”).
ex.consExitLess: In the column “{{scCons}}” {{erloesK}} remain from the sale, which is {{diffErloes}} less than planned ({{eqnDiff}}).
ex.consExitMore: In the column “{{scCons}}” {{erloesK}} remain from the sale, which is {{diffErloes}} more than planned.
ex.consNwLess: In the column “{{scCons}}” it would be {{nettoK}} net worth, so {{diffNetto}} less ({{eqnDiff}}).
ex.consNwMore: In the column “{{scCons}}” it would be {{nettoK}} net worth, so {{diffNetto}} more.
ex.riValue: At the end you own {{units}} handed-over {{w}} worth {{wert}}. A loan of {{kredit}} is still outstanding.
ex.riCash: There is {{cash}} in your account, which is the “{{kCash}}” at the top.
ex.riCashNeg: Your account is {{cashAbs}} in the red.
ex.riSumRound: Together that gives a rounded {{netto}} net worth.
ex.riConsLess: In the column “{{scCons}}” it is {{unitsK}} {{wK}} and {{nettoK}} net worth, so {{diffNetto}} less ({{eqnDiff}}).
ex.riConsMore: In the column “{{scCons}}” it is {{unitsK}} {{wK}} and {{nettoK}} net worth, so {{diffNetto}} more.
ex.p_unitsSold: An apartment that is sold on its own earlier also counts here.
ex.p_valueSold: An apartment that is sold on its own earlier no longer counts here.
ex.p_cfRound: apart from rounding by a few euros
ex.p_cfMore: you only see every year there after clicking “{{more}}” in the section “{{s3}}”
ex.p_cfHidden: although the table there does not show every year
ex.p_cfNeg: Negative means: you paid in overall.
ex.p_cfNegRi: Negative means: the apartments cost more overall than they brought in. The gap was taken from the money in your account within the strategy, for example from the rest of your starting capital{{negContrib}}.
ex.p_vatRepay: Where applicable, a partial repayment of the VAT refund is also deducted. It is due if a short-let apartment is sold within 10 years of handover.
ex.p_vatOpenItem: In the column “{{scBasis}}” the proceeds also include a VAT refund of {{vatOpen}}. It is still outstanding at the sale and is owed to you, reduced pro rata for the years still missing until 10 years after handover.
ex.aDeductVat: On the sale, {{whatDeduct}} are still deducted, {{abzug}} in total. On top of that comes a VAT refund of {{vatOpen}} that is still outstanding and owed to you. What remains is {{erloes}} ({{eqnExit}}), which is the row “{{scExit}}”.
ex.aVatOpen: This includes a VAT refund of {{vatOpen}} that is still outstanding at the sale and owed to you.
ex.p_cfSum: For “{{scBasis}}” this is the sum of the column “{{tNet}}” in the section “{{s5}}” over all years{{sumNote}}.
ex.p_clamp: Note: your plan assumes {{clampList}}. The table sets such values to at least 0 % in all three columns. That is why the numbers in “{{scBasis}}” do not exactly match the rest of the page here.

m.rangeExit: Depending on how the market develops, between {{erloesK}} (“{{scCons}}”) and {{erloesO}} (“{{scOpt}}”) remain for you from the sale. The plan is {{erloes}}.
m.range: Depending on how the market develops, your net worth at the end lies between {{nettoK}} (“{{scCons}}”) and {{nettoO}} (“{{scOpt}}”). The plan is {{netto}}.
m.dropExit: If the market runs as in “{{scCons}}”, about {{dropPctExit}} % less than planned remains for you after the sale.
m.drop: If the market runs as in “{{scCons}}”, you end up with about {{dropPct}} % less net worth than planned.
m.irrPos: Even in the column “{{scCons}}” the return per year is above zero at {{irrK}}. In this model your money would still come back with growth, just more slowly than planned ({{irrB}}).
m.irrNegB: Already in the column “{{scBasis}}” the return per year is below zero at {{irrB}}. Under these assumptions you would get back less in total than you put in.
m.irrNegK: In the column “{{scCons}}” the return per year is below zero at {{irrK}}. Under these assumptions you would get back less in total than you put in.
m.cfNegK: In the column “{{scCons}}”, “{{scCf}}” is negative: over the whole period you would have to add {{cfK}} out of your own pocket. You need a reserve for that.
m.total: If you add “{{scExit}}” and “{{scCf}}” together, {{gesB}} reach you in the column “{{scBasis}}” ({{eqnB}}), {{gesK}} in “{{scCons}}” and {{gesO}} in “{{scOpt}}”.
m.unitsK: With a development as in “{{scCons}}” there is only room for {{unitsK}} instead of {{units}} apartments. Less appreciation means less additional credit from the bank. Lower rents and higher interest mean less surplus for further purchases.
m.unitsOSame: In the column “{{scOpt}}” you end up with exactly as many apartments as planned ({{unitsO}}). The advantage there lies in the higher value, not in more apartments.
m.unitsOLess: In the column “{{scOpt}}” you even end up with fewer apartments than planned ({{unitsO}} instead of {{units}}), partly because further apartments also get more expensive faster there. Your net worth is still higher.
m.allSame: All three columns show the same numbers here.
m.allSameWhy: By {{y}} none of your apartments has been handed over yet. The appreciation, rent and interest of the columns only take effect from handover.
m.allSameSale: In the model an apartment under construction is sold for the amount of the instalments already paid.
m.irrSame: Even in the column “{{scCons}}” the return per year is above zero at {{irrK}}. Rounded, that is practically level with the plan.
m.unitsOMore: In the column “{{scOpt}}” there is room for {{unitsO}} instead of {{units}} apartments. More appreciation means more additional credit from the bank. Higher rents and lower interest mean more surplus for further purchases.
m.unitsKMore: In the column “{{scCons}}” you even end up with more apartments than planned ({{unitsK}} instead of {{units}}), partly because further apartments also get more expensive more slowly there. Your net worth there is still lower.

pitfalls.notWorst: “{{scCons}}” is not the worst case. Falling prices, long vacancies or much higher interest rates are not included.
pitfalls.noProb: The three columns are not probabilities. Nobody knows which development will come, and reality can also lie outside them.
pitfalls.twoPots: Net worth and “{{scCf}}” are two separate pots: the cash flow has already flowed over the years and is not part of the net worth.
pitfalls.inWorth: Do not add “{{scCf}}” to the net worth. With reinvestment the cash flow is already included in it.
pitfalls.beforeSale: The net worth is the position before the sale. What really remains after costs and taxes is shown in “{{scExit}}”. You find the details in the section “{{s10}}”.
pitfalls.notYield: “{{scIrr}}” is not the rental yield (annual rent divided by purchase price). It takes into account the loan, costs, taxes, appreciation and when each payment flows.
pitfalls.noSaleCosts: Without a sale, no selling costs and no taxes on a sale are deducted in net worth and “{{scIrr}}”. If you sold at the end, less would remain.
pitfalls.unitsDiff: The row “{{scUnits}}” counts all purchased apartments. At the top, “{{kUnits}}” shows {{top}}, because only apartments that have been handed over and not yet sold count there.
pitfalls.rateDay1: The higher interest in “{{scCons}}” applies in the model from the first day to all bank loans, not only to a later follow-up financing.
pitfalls.noSaleCostsRest: For the apartments you still own at the end, no selling costs and no taxes on a sale are deducted in net worth and “{{scIrr}}”. If you sold them, less would remain.
pitfalls.season: If one of your apartments calculates its rent with the season model, “{{scCons}}” is milder for it than the name suggests: its rent is not cut, it only rises more slowly.

sensitivity.heading: How to read the boxes
sensitivity.intro: Only one single assumption changes here: how much your apartments rise in value per year. Each box is a complete run of your strategy up to {{lastYear}}, with {{list}} % appreciation per year. Rents, interest and costs stay as planned.{{plan}}

pct.label: Percentage at the top
pct.text: The assumed appreciation per year. It applies to all apartments, including the ones the model buys in addition. {{pgNote}}

units.label: Large number
units.text: How many apartments you own at the end that have been handed over and not sold, including further purchases.

worth.label: Amount below
worth.text: Your net worth at the end: property value minus the loan outstanding plus money in your account. Costs and taxes of a sale are not deducted.

ex.p_planSame: The highlighted box with {{app}} % is your plan. It shows the same numbers as the column “{{scBasis}}” in the table above.
ex.p_planHl: The highlighted box with {{app}} % matches your planned appreciation.
ex.p_planNone: Your planned appreciation of {{app}} % is not one of the boxes, so none is highlighted.
ex.p_pgLinked: In the model the purchase prices of further apartments rise at the same pace.
ex.p_pgFixed: The purchase prices of further apartments always rise by {{pg}} % per year here.
ex.p_dropWhy: In the model, further apartments also get more expensive with appreciation. Each further purchase then needs more equity.
ex.base0: Without any appreciation ({{a0}} %) you would have {{u0}} {{w0}} and {{n0}} net worth at the end.
ex.base: With {{a0}} % appreciation you would have {{u0}} {{w0}} and {{n0}} net worth at the end.
ex.plan: With your planned {{aP}} % it is {{uP}} {{wP}} and {{nP}}. The difference between {{a0}} % and your planned {{aP}} % is {{diffSens}} here ({{eqnPlan}}).{{unitsNote}}
ex.span: Between the box with {{a0}} % and the one with {{aN}} % lie {{span}} of net worth ({{eqnSpan}}).
ex.p_planUnits: Note that this does not compare the same apartments: at {{a0}} % you end up with {{u0}} instead of {{uP}} {{wP}}.
ex.planLess: With your planned {{aP}} % it is {{uP}} {{wP}} and {{nP}}, which is {{diffSensLess}} less than at {{a0}} % ({{eqnPlanLess}}).

m.drop: Worth noting: with {{aH}} % appreciation you end up with fewer apartments ({{uH}}) than with {{aL}} % ({{uL}}), but with more net worth ({{nH}} instead of {{nL}}). This is not a calculation error.{{why}} What matters for your wealth is the euro amount, not the number of apartments.
m.belowEk: Without appreciation your net worth at the end would be {{n0}}, below your starting capital of {{ek}}. The strategy then depends heavily on appreciation.
m.ratio: The further apart the amounts in the boxes are, the more your result depends on how values develop. And nobody can predict that. In your case the net worth with {{aN}} % is about {{ratio}} times as high as with {{a0}} %.
m.dropLess: Worth noting: at {{bH}} % you end up with fewer apartments ({{vH}} instead of {{vL}}) and even less net worth ({{mH}} instead of {{mL}}) than at {{bL}} %. With more appreciation, further apartments also get more expensive in the model, so it buys fewer of them. Here that weighs more than the higher growth in value.

pitfalls.onlyOne: Only appreciation changes here. In the table above, “{{scCons}}” and “{{scOpt}}” shift several assumptions at once. That is why the boxes do not exactly match those columns, even if the percentage is the same.
pitfalls.zeroNotWorst: 0 % is not the worst case. Falling prices are not included here.
pitfalls.moreUnits: More apartments do not automatically mean more wealth. Always compare the amount below.
pitfalls.notCash: Net worth is not an account balance. What is tied up in the apartments only becomes money through a sale.

portfolio.heading: How to read the staircase and the table
portfolio.intro: The staircase in the chart shows for each year how many apartments you have in the portfolio. In the portfolio means: handed over and ready to let. The years from {{firstYear}} to {{lastYear}} run across, the number runs up. If the staircase goes up, at least one apartment was handed over that year. If it goes down, one was sold. The table below also shows value, loan and equity for the years, each at the end of the year.

line.label: Blue staircase
line.text: Apartments in the portfolio at the end of the year. Purchased apartments that are still being built only count from the year of their handover. On a computer you see the exact number when you move the mouse over a year.

buy.label: Green dot
buy.text: A year in which the model buys a further apartment (purchase contract). Your own first purchases have no dot.

sell.label: Coral dot
sell.text: A year in which an apartment is sold. From that year on it no longer counts.

year.label: Year
year.text: The calendar year. At first you only see the key years: the first, the 5th and the 10th year, the last one and every year with a further purchase or a sale. With “{{more}}” you see every year.

owned.label: purchased
owned.text: Apartments with a signed purchase contract, even if they are still being built. Sold apartments no longer count from the year of sale.

units.label: in the portfolio
units.text: Of these, the apartments already handed over. Only they bring rent and have a value in the column “{{tValue}}”.

value.label: Value
value.text: Market value of the handed-over apartments, projected with the assumed appreciation of {{app}} % per year. Apartments under construction are not included here yet.

debt.label: Loan
debt.text: All debts open at the end of the year: the rest of the bank loans, additional loans the bank grants on apartments already handed over (refinancing), instalments still owed to the developer after handover and, if needed, a bridging loan that covers instalments until the bank loan is paid out.

equity.label: Equity
equity.text: Value minus loan. This is the part of the apartments that economically belongs to you. It grows when the value rises and the loan is repaid (repayment is the part of the instalment that reduces the debt). A new loan for a further purchase reduces it at first, because the purchased apartment only counts towards the value from its handover.

ex.p_ownSteps: The handovers of your own apartments are steps too.
ex.buy: In {{buyYear}} the model buys the first further apartment (first green dot).
ex.buyLater: It is handed over in {{readyYear}}. Only from then on does it count in the staircase and in the column “{{tUnits}}”.
ex.buySame: It is handed over in the same year and counts straight away.
ex.last: In the last row ({{y}}) {{units}} {{w}} {{verb}} been handed over, worth {{wert}} together. A loan of {{kredit}} sits on them: {{eqnLast}} equity.
ex.firstNone1: In {{fy}}, {{owned}} {{wF}} {{verbO}} been purchased but not yet handed over. It is still being built and therefore does not appear in value and equity yet.
ex.firstNone: In {{fy}}, {{owned}} {{wF}} {{verbO}} been purchased, but none of them has been handed over yet. They are still being built and therefore do not appear in value and equity yet.
ex.firstSome: In {{fy}}, {{owned}} {{wF}} {{verbO}} been purchased, but only {{fUnits}} {{verbF}} been handed over. The others are still being built and therefore do not appear in value and equity yet.
ex.p_oppHint: On paper a further purchase would be possible in {{oy}}, see the box in the section “{{s4}}”.

m.grow: Your {{start}} apartments become {{end}} apartments in the portfolio by {{lastYear}}.
m.grow1: Your one apartment becomes {{end}} apartments in the portfolio by {{lastYear}}.
m.noBuy: Under these assumptions the model does not buy a further apartment. The staircase only shows when your own apartments are handed over{{sold}}.
m.eqPct: At the end about {{pct}} % of the property value belongs to you, the rest is still loan.
m.p_cash: there is still {{cash}} in your account
m.p_comm: {{committed}} is tied up in apartments under construction
m.nwPlus: Your net worth at the end ({{nw}}) is higher than the equity in the last row because {{parts}}: {{eqnNw}}.
m.nwMinus: Your net worth at the end ({{nw}}) is lower than the equity in the last row because your account is {{cashAbs}} in the red: {{eqnNw}}.
m.debtUp: If the loan rises from one year to the next even though it is being repaid, new loans have been added: from a refinancing, or the bank loan of a further apartment once it is handed over. This is planned, but it increases your debts.
m.noBuyOff: Automatic further purchases are switched off in your plan. That is why the model does not buy a further apartment.{{oppNote}} The staircase only shows when your own apartments are handed over{{sold}}.

pitfalls.stepIsHandover: The staircase rises in the year of handover, not in the year of purchase. So not every step is a further purchase.
pitfalls.greenNoRent: A green dot does not mean the new apartment brings rent straight away. The model buys further apartments under construction, rent only flows after handover.
pitfalls.ownedNotUnits: “{{tOwned}}” is not “{{tUnits}}”: an apartment under construction brings no rent yet and has no value in this table yet.
pitfalls.earlyEquity: In the first years the equity looks small even though you have already paid a lot. The money you have already paid for your own apartments under construction is not gone: it is in the building site and counts as tied-up capital in the net worth.
pitfalls.notCash: Equity is not money in your account. You can only get at it through a sale or a new loan.
pitfalls.estimate: The value is a projection with the assumed appreciation, not a valuation report and not a sale price.
pitfalls.model: From the first further purchase on, model apartments are part of the numbers: calculated apartments based on your apartments, not a specific offer.

recycling.heading: How to read the factor, the path and the table
recycling.intro: This section shows where the money for further apartments comes from. At the top is the “{{recycleLabel}}”, below it “{{journeyTitle}}” with its stations{{tablePart}}. “Cash pot” here means your account within the strategy. It collects {{kasse}}. “Equity” means two things here: at purchase, the money you put in yourself (the bank provides the rest), and at the stations, value minus loan, i.e. the part of the apartments that belongs to you.

factor.label: Capital recycling factor
factor.text: The large number ({{faktor}}×). It divides your own money that flows again as equity into further apartments in the model by your starting capital of {{ek}}. Own money here means money that already belongs to you, i.e. {{kasse}}. Money from refinancing (additional loans on apartments already handed over) does not count, because it is a new loan. Only what flows in the purchase year of a further apartment is counted. Instalments that fall due later are missing. The number is rounded to one decimal place. 1,0× would mean: own money equal to your starting capital works a second time.

jStart.label: Dein Startkapital
jStart.text: The money you bring in at the start.

jFirst.label: 2 Wohnungen
jFirst.text: This much money flows into your first purchases: equity plus purchase costs (in the model 1 % of the purchase price including VAT). {{bank}} {{restNote}}

jFirst1.label: Erste Wohnung
jFirst1.text: This much money flows into your first purchase: equity plus purchase costs (in the model 1 % of the purchase price including VAT). {{bank}} {{restNote}}

jRents.label: Miete, Tilgung, Wertzuwachs
jRents.text: Despite its name, this amount is only the sum of all rental income over the whole period, from all apartments, including the further ones. It is before deducting costs, interest, repayment and taxes. Repayment and appreciation are in the next station.

jEq.label: Eigenkapital wächst
jEq.text: This is how much higher the equity in all apartments at the end (value minus loan) is than the amount at “{{jFirstLabel}}” (station 2), i.e. {{firstMoney}}. The growth comes from repayment and appreciation. Added to this is your own money that flowed as equity into further apartments. New loans from refinancing are already deducted.{{neg}}

jRefi.label: Refinanzierung
jRefi.text: The sum of all additional loans the bank grants on apartments already handed over (refinancing). This is possible when an apartment has risen in value and is partly paid off. The money pays for further purchases. It is a new loan, not a profit: it increases your debts and is serviced with interest and repayment from the rents.

jBuys.label: Weitere Wohnungen
jBuys.text: Not the purchase price and not the full equity of these apartments. Only your own money that flows in during each purchase year on top of the new loan is counted. Exactly this number is in the “{{recycleLabel}}”.

jNet.label: Netto-Vermögen
jNet.text: Your result at the end: equity in the apartments plus money in your account{{jComm}}. The same number as “{{kNet}}” at the top.

year.label: Year
year.text: The year in which the event takes place. Within a year the rows appear in this order: sale, refinancing, purchase.

source.label: Property
source.text: For a refinancing, the apartment on which the loan is taken out. For a sale, the apartment sold. For a purchase, the new apartment. “Modellwohnung 1”, “Modellwohnung 2” and so on (model apartment 1, 2 ...) are calculated apartments based on your apartments, not a specific offer.

amount.label: Amount
amount.text: Green amounts come in, coral amounts with a minus go out. For a refinancing, the size of the new loan. It is only taken out for the purchase in the same year. For a sale, what remains after loan, costs and taxes. For a purchase, the equity for the new apartment including purchase costs. The bank finances {{ltv}} % of the total price including VAT and furniture.{{rates}}

reinvested.label: of which reinvested
reinvested.text: For a refinancing the whole amount, because the loan is only taken out for the purchase in the same year. For a purchase, the part that comes from the new loan of that year. It can be slightly higher than the amount, because the loan then also covers costs that the new apartment and the new loan already cause in the purchase year. A dash means: no money from a refinancing. So the column only counts borrowed money.{{saleDash}}

ex.kStart: the rest of your starting capital
ex.p_table: and finally the table with every single money movement
ex.p_bankAll: The bank pays the rest of the purchase price.
ex.p_bankNone: There is no bank loan for this.
ex.p_bankSome: The bank pays the rest where planned.
ex.p_restLeft: What is left of your starting capital ({{left}}) stays in your account.
ex.p_restOver: That is more than your starting capital of {{ek}}, because the purchase costs come on top.
ex.p_eqNeg: A minus here means the equity has gone down.
ex.p_jComm: plus instalments already paid for apartments under construction
ex.evRefi: “{{evRefi}}” (refinancing): the bank grants an additional loan on an apartment already handed over.
ex.evSale: “{{evSale}}” (sale): an apartment is sold because a year of sale is planned for it.
ex.evBuy: “{{evBuy}}” (purchase): the model buys a further apartment.
ex.p_rates: In the model this equity is paid in instalments over the construction period. The table shows it in one sum in the purchase year.
ex.factor: In your case {{rec}} of your own money flows again as equity into further apartments. {{rec}} divided by your starting capital of {{ek}} gives a rounded {{faktor}}×.
ex.journey: This is how the stations fit together: {{own}} {{firstWord}} plus {{built}} growth give {{eqEnd}} equity in the apartments at the end ({{eqnJ}}).
ex.journeyNeg: This is how the stations fit together: of {{own}} {{firstWord}}, {{eqEnd}} of equity in the apartments is left at the end ({{eqnJ}}).
ex.p_comm: and {{committed}} of instalments already paid for apartments under construction
ex.net: Add {{cash}} in your account{{comm}}. Together that is {{nw}} net worth ({{eqnN}}).
ex.netNeg: Your account is {{cashAbs}} in the red{{comm}}. That leaves {{nw}} net worth ({{eqnN}}).
ex.rents: Do not add the {{rents}} of rents: costs, interest, repayment and taxes were paid from them over the years. Whatever was left is in the account or in further apartments.
ex.rentsNoBuy: Do not add the {{rents}} of rents: costs, interest, repayment and taxes were paid from them over the years. Whatever was left is in the account.
ex.tRefi1: In the table for {{y}}: the bank grants an additional loan of {{refiY}} on an apartment already handed over (row “{{evRefi}}”).
ex.tRefiN: In the table for {{y}}: the bank grants additional loans of {{refiY}} in total on {{nRefi}} apartments already handed over (rows “{{evRefi}}”).
ex.tBuy: In the same year the model buys a further apartment. It needs {{eq}} of equity for this (row “{{evBuy}}”).
ex.tRest: {{reinv}} of it comes from the new loan, the remaining {{rest}} from your cash pot ({{eqnT}}).
ex.tExact: The new loan covers this equity exactly.
ex.tOver: The new loan covers this equity in full. The remaining {{over}} covers costs that the new apartment and the new loan already cause in the purchase year, so that the reserve stays in the account ({{eqnT}}).
ex.tCash: In {{y2}} the model buys a further apartment without any new loan: the {{eq2}} of equity comes entirely from your cash pot. That is why a dash is shown there under “{{tReinvested}}”.
ex.p_below1Refi: New loans from refinancing pay part of the equity.
ex.p_splitFactor: The “{{recycleLabel}}” only counts {{rec}} of this, because it only records the money of each purchase year. Instalments that fall due in later years are missing there.
ex.p_gainContrib: Your monthly top-ups are not deducted from this.
ex.firstMoneyN: the money for your first purchases
ex.firstMoney1: the money for your first purchase
ex.p_saleDash: A sale always shows a dash: the proceeds go into your cash pot and can pay for later purchases, but the column only counts money from refinancing.
ex.rentsNeg: Do not add the {{rents}} of rents: costs, interest, repayment and taxes were paid from them over the years. Nothing of it is left in the account at the end, it is even in the red.
ex.p_below1Count: In addition, the factor counts neither money from refinancing nor instalments that only fall due after the purchase year.
ex.p_below1CountNoRates: In addition, the factor does not count money from refinancing.

m.noBuy: Under these assumptions the model does not buy a further apartment. That is why the factor shows {{faktor}}×: no money is reused. Your wealth then develops with your first apartments alone.
m.zero: The factor shows {{faktor}}× here, even though the model buys further apartments. The reason: the equity due in the purchase year is paid there entirely or almost entirely by new loans. The factor only counts own money that flows on top of that.
m.below1: A factor below 1 means: less own money than your starting capital works a second time. Most of the purchase prices of further apartments are paid by bank loans ({{ltv}} % of the total price).
m.above1: A factor of {{faktor}}× means: own money of {{faktor}} times your starting capital flows into apartments again over the years. That is not a profit but money that is used more than once.
m.refi: The {{refi}} at “{{jRefiLabel}}” are borrowed. These loans are serviced with interest and repayment from the rents. Whatever is still open at the end is part of the number “{{kDebt}}” at the top ({{debt}}).
m.split: According to the table, {{eqSum}} of equity flows into {{n}} further apartments in total. {{refiSum}} of it comes from new loans, {{restSum}} from your cash pot ({{eqnS}}).
m.split1: According to the table, {{eqSum}} of equity flows into the further apartment. {{refiSum}} of it comes from new loans, {{restSum}} from your cash pot ({{eqnS}}).
m.splitCash: According to the table, {{eqSum}} of equity flows into {{n}} further apartments in total. It comes entirely from your cash pot, no new loans were needed for it.
m.splitCash1: According to the table, {{eqSum}} of equity flows into the further apartment. It comes entirely from your cash pot, no new loan was needed for it.
m.sale: In {{ys}} an apartment is sold. After loan, costs and taxes, {{net}} remain. This money goes into your cash pot and can pay for further purchases. Under “{{tReinvested}}” this row still shows a dash, because the column only counts money from refinancing.
m.gain: Compared with your starting capital of {{ek}}, your net worth has grown by {{gain}} by {{lastYear}}, before costs and taxes of a sale ({{eqnG}}).
m.loss: Compared with your starting capital of {{ek}}, your net worth has fallen by {{lossAbs}} by {{lastYear}} ({{eqnG}}).
m.noBuyOff: Automatic further purchases are switched off in your plan. That is why the model does not buy a further apartment.{{oppNote}} That is why the factor shows {{faktor}}×: no money is reused. Your wealth then develops with your first apartments alone.

pitfalls.notReturn: The factor is not a return and not a profit. 2,0× would not mean that your money has doubled.
pitfalls.higherNotBetter: A higher factor is not automatically better. It only says how much money is reused, not how well it earns.
pitfalls.noSum: Do not add up the amounts of the stations. They measure different things: positions at one point in time, sums over many years and new loans.
pitfalls.rentsOnly: “{{jRents}}” only shows the sum of the rents. Repayment and appreciation are in “{{jEq}}”.
pitfalls.refiNotProfit: Refinancing is not part of the factor, even though it helps pay for further purchases. A green amount at “{{evRefi}}” is not a profit but borrowed money.{{saleGreen}}
pitfalls.sameMoney: Do not add up refinancing and purchase in the same year. It is the same money: once coming in as a loan and once going out into the new apartment.
pitfalls.notPrice: The amount for a purchase is not the purchase price, only the equity including purchase costs.
pitfalls.twoThings: “{{tReinvested}}” counts borrowed money from refinancing, the factor only own money. So the two measure different things.

opportunity.heading: What this box means
opportunity.intro: The box shows the first year in which the model can finance a further apartment on paper. It checks: is the money in your account above the minimum reserve, together with the additional loan the bank could grant, enough for the equity of a further apartment? The minimum reserve is the money that should always stay in the account, {{reserve}} in your case.{{probe}}

title.label: Heading
title.text: The year in question. “On paper” means: the numbers work out under the assumptions chosen. It is not a commitment from the bank.

cap.label: Additional borrowing capacity
cap.text: This much additional credit the bank could grant on paper this year on your apartments that are already handed over and fully paid to the developer: up to {{ltv}} % of the value the bank applies{{bvfNote}}, minus the loans already on them.{{utilNote}} These {{ltv}} % are called the loan-to-value ratio: the share of the value that a bank lends at most. The number is not money you have, but money you could borrow.

price.label: Purchase price of the next apartment in the model
price.text: The purchase price of the model apartment in this year, without VAT and without furniture. Model apartment means: a calculated apartment {{basis}}, whose price rises by {{pg}} % every year. Not a specific offer.

eq.label: Equity required
eq.text: What you would have to raise yourself for this apartment: the part of the total price (including VAT and furniture) that the bank does not finance, plus purchase costs (in the model 1 % of the purchase price including VAT). The calculation assumes a bank loan of {{ltv}} % of the total price.

ex.p_bvf: (in your case {{bvf}} % of the market value)
ex.p_target: based on the apartment selected for this
ex.p_avg: based on the average of your apartments
ex.base: In {{y}} the bank could lend up to {{cap}} in addition on your handed-over apartments on paper. A further apartment at the model price of {{price}} would need {{req}} of equity.
ex.baseNoCap: In {{y}} there is no room yet on paper for an additional loan on your apartments ({{cap}}). A further apartment at the model price of {{price}} would need {{req}} of equity.
ex.execExact: The model carries out this purchase: it is the row “{{evBuy}}” {{y}} in the table above, with exactly this amount.
ex.exec: The model carries out this purchase: it is the row “{{evBuy}}” {{y}} in the table above.
ex.usedPart: Of the possible {{cap}}, the model only takes {{used}} as a new loan for it.
ex.usedFull: For this the model takes {{used}} as a new loan, i.e. the whole borrowing capacity.
ex.noLoan: No new loan is needed for this, the equity comes from your cash pot.
ex.notExec: The model does not carry out this purchase on its own.
ex.p_probe: The model also runs the purchase as a trial: the minimum reserve has to hold in the purchase year and in every following year. Otherwise the model does not buy, and the year does not appear here.
ex.notExecOff: The model does not carry out this purchase, because automatic further purchases are switched off. Whether your reserve holds in every year afterwards has not been checked.

m.exec: So the box does not show an extra purchase on top. It explains why the first further purchase in {{y}} is possible.
m.notExec: This apartment is an additional option that is not part of your numbers. If you bought it, you would take on new loans: the bank loan for the apartment and, if your account is not enough, part of the {{cap}}. Whether that is affordable also depends on your income and on the bank's assessment.
m.reqGtCap: The equity required is higher than the possible additional loan. So the money in your account above the minimum reserve of {{reserve}} has to cover at least {{diffCap}} ({{eqnC}}).
m.reqNoCap: Because no additional loan is possible, the whole equity required has to come from the money in your account above the minimum reserve of {{reserve}}.

pitfalls.noPromise: “Possible on paper” is not a financing commitment. The bank checks income, creditworthiness and value itself.
pitfalls.notBalance: The borrowing capacity is not a credit balance. Every euro of it would be a new loan with interest and repayment.
pitfalls.modelPrice: The model price is a calculated figure, not an offer for a specific apartment.
pitfalls.moreThanShare: Do not simply take {{eqPct}} % of the purchase price in the box: the price there is without VAT and without furniture, while the equity required includes both plus the purchase costs.
